teile.einleitung: The compass jellyfish is a jellyfish from the Atlantic, the North Sea and the Mediterranean. It gets its name from the brown stripes on its bell, which are reminiscent of a compass rose. It can sting with its tentacles, but for people it is usually only unpleasant.
wichtigste: The compass jellyfish is called Chrysaora hysoscella in science.
It belongs to the true jellyfish and thus to the cnidarians.
On its bell it has 16 brown, V-shaped stripes like a compass rose.
Its bell usually grows to about 30 centimetres across.
It eats plankton, fish larvae and other jellyfish.
A touch stings and burns on the skin.
Its body consists for the most part of water.

abschnitte.text: The bell of the compass jellyfish is transparent, whitish to yellowish. From the centre, 16 brown, **V-shaped stripes** run to the edge, so that the pattern resembles a compass. 24 thin tentacles hang from the edge of the bell, and four long, frilly **oral arms** wave beneath it. Like all jellyfish, it has neither brain nor heart nor bones.

Compass jellyfish live in the north-east Atlantic, in the North Sea, in the English Channel and in the Mediterranean. They mostly drift near the coast in the upper part of the water. In summer and autumn they are often washed up on beaches in large numbers. In the Baltic Sea they hardly occur because of the low salt content.

The compass jellyfish is a **predator**. With its tentacles it catches small crustaceans, fish eggs, fish larvae and also other jellyfish. The prey is paralysed by **stinging cells**, which fire tiny venom threads. The oral arms then carry the food to the mouth opening under the bell.

Compass jellyfish have an **alternation of generations**. A larva turns into a small, fixed polyp on the sea floor. This pinches off many tiny young jellyfish, which swim away and grow into large jellyfish. What is special is that compass jellyfish are first male and later female.

Contact with the tentacles leads to burning, red patches of skin, which usually fade after some time. Even washed-up jellyfish can still sting, so you should not touch them. You should rinse the spot with seawater and not rub it. If symptoms are severe, a doctor or the lifeguard can help.

The compass jellyfish lives only in salt water and does not occur in Switzerland. Swiss children are most likely to meet it on holiday by the Mediterranean or the North Sea. In some Swiss lakes, however, there is a tiny **freshwater jellyfish** that grows only about two centimetres across. It is completely harmless to people.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal group with stinging cells, for example jellyfish, corals and sea anemones.
A cell that fires a tiny venom thread when touched.
A fixed life form of cnidarians that looks like a small tube.
A long, movable grasping arm.

gewusst: A jellyfish consists of about 95 per cent water or more.
Leatherback turtles like to eat jellyfish and tolerate the sting venom.
Small fish sometimes hide among the tentacles of jellyfish to be safe from enemies.

teile.einleitung: Lapland is a large region in the far north of Europe, lying for the most part north of the Arctic Circle. Here live the Sámi, a people who traditionally live with reindeer. In summer the sun does not set for weeks, and in winter it stays dark for a long time.
wichtigste: Lapland lies in the north of Norway, Sweden, Finland and Russia.
The Sámi are the indigenous people of this area and call their land Sápmi.
Many Sámi still keep reindeer today.
A large part of Lapland lies north of the Arctic Circle.
In summer there is the midnight sun, in winter the polar night.
On clear winter nights the northern lights often glow in the sky.
Typical animals are reindeer, elk, wolverine and Arctic fox.

abschnitte.text: Lapland is not a state of its own, but a region that stretches across four countries. It includes the north of **Norway**, Sweden and Finland as well as the Kola Peninsula in Russia. In Finland there is even a region that is officially called Lapland, with the capital Rovaniemi. The Sámi themselves call their whole area of settlement **Sápmi**.

Lapland consists of wide coniferous forests, bogs, countless lakes and bare mountains, the **fjells**. Further north hardly any trees grow, and there the **tundra** begins with mosses, lichens and dwarf shrubs. The winters are long and very cold, often far below minus 20 degrees. The summers are short, but bright and full of mosquitoes.

The best-known animal of Lapland is the **reindeer**, which roams here in large herds. Alongside it live elk, brown bears, wolves, lynx and the powerful **wolverine**. In the mountains you find Arctic foxes, ptarmigan and the small lemmings. Many migratory birds come in summer to breed in the bright bogs.

The **Sámi** have lived in Lapland for thousands of years. In the past many families moved back and forth with their reindeer herds between summer and winter pastures. They have languages of their own, a colourful costume and the special singing called joik. Today most Sámi live in houses and work in quite ordinary jobs, but reindeer herding remains important for their culture.

North of the Arctic Circle the sun does not set at all in midsummer, which is called the **midnight sun**. In midwinter, by contrast, it does not rise above the horizon for weeks, which is the **polar night**. In return you can often see green northern lights dancing on clear nights. For people from Switzerland this change of light and darkness is very unfamiliar.

Besides reindeer herding, people in Lapland live from timber, hydropower and mining, for example from the iron ore at Kiruna in Sweden. **Tourism** is becoming more and more important. Visitors ride in dog or reindeer sledges, watch the northern lights or visit Santa Claus Village near Rovaniemi. Many Swiss families also travel there in winter.

begriffe.erklaerung: An imaginary line on the Earth, north of which there are midnight sun and polar night.
A cold landscape almost without trees, with mosses and lichens.
The indigenous people of Lapland with their own language and culture.
The traditional singing of the Sámi.

gewusst: The word ‘Lapps’ for the Sámi is now regarded as derogatory, and they wish to be called Sámi.
Reindeer can smell lichens under the snow and scrape them free with their hooves.
In Finnish Lapland there are about as many reindeer as people.

teile.einleitung: Bony fish are by far the largest group of fish. Their skeleton is made of true bone, and their gills are protected by a hard cover. Almost all fish in Swiss lakes and rivers, from perch to whitefish, are bony fish.
wichtigste: Bony fish have a skeleton of bone and not of cartilage.
Whitefish, perch, trout and pike are bony fish.
With over 30,000 species they are the most species-rich group of vertebrates.
A gill cover protects their gills.
Many have a swim bladder with which they can hover in the water.
Their skin is usually covered with thin, overlapping scales.
They live in seas, lakes, rivers and even in hot springs and caves.

abschnitte.text: Bony fish are fish with an internal skeleton of hardened tissue. In this they differ from the **cartilaginous fish** such as sharks and rays. With well over 30,000 species they make up the largest part of all fish. Their shapes range from the flat flatfish through the long seahorse to the round pufferfish.

The gills of bony fish lie under a movable **gill cover**. Many have a **swim bladder**, a gas-filled organ with which they regulate their buoyancy. In this way they can hover in the water without constantly swimming. Most have thin scales that lie over one another like roof tiles and grow with the fish.

Almost all bony fish are **ray-finned fish**; their fins are supported by thin bony rays. They include carp, salmon, perch and tuna. A small group are the **lobe-finned fish** with strong, fleshy fins, such as coelacanths and lungfish. From ancestors of the lobe-finned fish, the first land vertebrates developed around 370 million years ago.

Most bony fish lay very many small eggs, the **spawn**, into the water. The males usually release their sperm into the water as well, so that fertilisation takes place outside the body. A carp can lay hundreds of thousands of eggs. Some species such as the stickleback build nests and guard their brood, while others such as the guppy give birth to live young.

In Swiss waters live around 70 native fish species, all of which are bony fish. Especially well known are the **whitefish**, which are fished in many lakes, and the perch, the river perch. Added to these are the brown trout, grayling, pike, carp and chub. Some species such as the salmon have disappeared from Switzerland and are to be reintroduced.

The heaviest bony fish is the **ocean sunfish**, which can weigh over two tonnes. Among the longest is the oarfish, which grows to several metres long. The sailfish is one of the fastest swimmers in the sea. There are also tiny species that measure barely a centimetre when fully grown.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bony plate that protects the gills of bony fish.
A gas-filled organ with which a fish hovers in the water.
The largest group of bony fish, with fins made of thin bony rays.
The eggs of fish and amphibians.

gewusst: Strictly speaking, we humans too are descendants of bony fish, because all land vertebrates descend from lobe-finned fish.
From the scales of some fish you can tell how old they are, as with tree rings.

teile.einleitung: An avalanche dog is a specially trained rescue dog that tracks down people under the snow. With its fine nose it smells buried people even through several metres of snow. In the Swiss Alps, avalanche dogs are a firm part of mountain rescue.
wichtigste: Avalanche dogs search for people buried by avalanches.
They smell people even deep under the snow.
A dog can search an area much faster than many people.
After an avalanche every minute counts.
Avalanche dogs are often flown to the scene by helicopter.
Today they are usually German shepherds, Labradors or Border collies.
The most famous rescue dog in Switzerland was the St Bernard Barry.

abschnitte.text: Avalanche dogs are **rescue dogs** that specialise in searching in snow. When an avalanche has buried people, they run across the avalanche debris and sniff for human scent. If they have a trace, they begin to bark and dig at that spot. Then the rescuers know exactly where they have to shovel.

Dogs have many millions more smell cells than humans. The scent of a person rises through the loose snow, and the dog picks it up at the surface. In this way it often finds buried people even at a depth of several metres. A well-trained dog searches an avalanche field about as fast as very many people with **avalanche probes** together.

Anyone lying under an avalanche has hardly any air left after a short time. In the first 15 minutes most buried people survive, after that the chances fall quickly. That is why ski tourers carry an **avalanche transceiver** with which companions can locate them at once. Avalanche dogs are especially important when someone had no such device with them.

In Switzerland the **Alpine Rettung Schweiz** (Swiss Alpine Rescue), together with partners, trains avalanche dogs and their handlers. In winter teams are ready in many mountain regions. In an alarm a helicopter, for example from Rega, often flies them directly to the scene. Dog and human train for this over years and must pass tests regularly.

Training begins playfully: a person hides in the snow, and the dog gets a reward on finding them, for example a toy. Later the hiding places become deeper and harder. An avalanche dog must also sit calmly in the helicopter and not let itself be distracted by the noise. Suitable are dogs that like to work, are brave and have plenty of stamina.

abschnitte.titel: Barry of the Great St Bernard
abschnitte.text: Over 200 years ago, dogs of the hospice on the **Great St Bernard** were already helping travellers in need. The St Bernard Barry is said to have saved over 40 people around 1800. His preserved hide stands today in the Natural History Museum of Bern. For modern avalanche searching St Bernards are too heavy, however, which is why lighter breeds are used today.

begriffe.erklaerung: A dog trained to find missing or buried people.
The heap of snow that is left lying after an avalanche.
A long pole with which rescuers prod in the snow for buried people.
The person who works with the dog and leads it.

gewusst: The famous little barrel round the neck of St Bernards is a legend, real rescue dogs did not wear one.
Avalanche dogs sometimes wear their own ear protection on helicopter flights.
Barry is so famous to this day that in the Valais a foundation with his name breeds St Bernards.

teile.einleitung: Cabbage whites are white butterflies whose caterpillars like to eat cabbage and related plants. In Switzerland they flutter through gardens, over meadows and fields from spring to autumn. Best known are the large white and the small white.
wichtigste: Cabbage whites are day-flying butterflies from the family of the whites.
Their wings are white with black tips and spots.
The caterpillars eat cabbage, rape, nasturtium and other cruciferous plants.
There is the large white and the small white, which are often confused.
In vegetable gardens the caterpillars can do a lot of damage.
They usually produce two to three generations a year.
A small parasitic wasp is one of their most important natural enemies.

abschnitte.text: Cabbage whites have white to cream-coloured **wings** with black tips on the forewings. The females also carry two black spots on each forewing, the males usually only one or none. The **large white** has a wingspan of about 5 to 6 centimetres. The **small white** is much smaller and has less strong black markings.

The caterpillars eat plants from the **cabbage family** (cruciferous plants), for example white cabbage, Brussels sprouts, broccoli, rape and mustard. They also like the nasturtium in the garden. These plants contain sharp mustard oils that put off many other insects. Cabbage whites are adapted to this and even recognise their food plants by this smell.

The female large white lays yellow eggs in groups on the underside of a leaf. Its caterpillars are yellowish-green with black spots and often feed together. The caterpillars of the small white, by contrast, are velvety green and live singly. After a few weeks the caterpillar pupates, and a new butterfly emerges from the **chrysalis**.

When many caterpillars sit on a head of cabbage, they eat the leaves down to the ribs. That is why cabbage whites are considered **pests** in vegetable growing. Gardeners often protect their plants with fine nets so that the butterflies cannot lay eggs. You can also pick off the eggs and caterpillars by hand.

The caterpillars store substances from the cabbage plants and therefore taste bad to many birds. An important enemy is the tiny **braconid wasp** Cotesia glomerata. It lays its eggs in the caterpillars, and the wasp larvae eat the caterpillar from the inside. Afterwards they spin themselves into small yellow cocoons next to the dead caterpillar.

Cabbage whites live in Europe, North Africa and large parts of Asia. The small white was accidentally introduced to North America in the 19th century and later also to Australia and New Zealand. Today it is one of the most widespread **butterflies** in the world. The large white is a migratory butterfly that can fly over long distances.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plant family with four petals in the shape of a cross, for example cabbage and rape.
The larva of a butterfly, which feeds and grows.
A resting stage in which the caterpillar changes into a butterfly.
A small wasp that lays its eggs in other insects.

gewusst: Cabbage whites can see ultraviolet light, and to them males and females therefore look much more different than they do to us.
A female large white can lay several hundred eggs.

teile.einleitung: Gills are the breathing organs of fish and many other water animals. With them the animals take oxygen from the water, just as we take it from the air with our lungs. Whether salmon, trout, carp or goldfish, all fish breathe with gills.
wichtigste: Fish breathe with gills.
Gills take up the oxygen dissolved in the water.
In bony fish the gills lie protected under the gill cover.
Gills consist of many fine plates with a rich blood supply.
Water flows in through the mouth and out again over the gills.
Tadpoles, mussels and crustaceans also have gills.
In air, gills collapse and no longer work.

abschnitte.text: **Gills** are breathing organs with which animals can breathe underwater. Water contains much less oxygen than air, so gills have to be very effective. All fish breathe with them, whether salmon, trout, lake trout, carp, catfish or goldfish. Many other water animals also have gills.

In bony fish, four **gill arches** sit on each side of the head. From them hang hundreds of fine gill filaments, threaded with tiny blood vessels. Because so much blood flows through them, healthy gills are bright red. A hard **gill cover** protects the delicate gills from outside.

The fish opens its mouth and takes in water. Then it closes it and pushes the water backwards over the gills, where it leaves again under the gill cover. In the process, oxygen passes from the water into the blood, and carbon dioxide passes into the water. Because blood and water flow in opposite directions, the exchange works especially well; this is called the **counter-current principle**.

Sharks and rays have no gill cover, but usually five to seven **gill slits** at the side. Some sharks have to keep swimming so that enough water flows over their gills. Some fish can also breathe air, for example lungfish. A fish out of water still suffocates, because its gill filaments stick together.

Frog tadpoles breathe with gills first and only later get lungs. The **axolotl**, a tailed amphibian from Mexico, keeps bushy gills on the outside of its head all its life. Mussels, crustaceans and the larvae of water insects such as mayflies also have gills. They look quite different, however.

At the fish market you recognise a fresh fish by its bright red gills. Fish need clean water with enough oxygen, otherwise they gasp for air at the surface. In warm summers the oxygen in lakes and rivers can become scarce, which is dangerous for fish. That is why an aquarium too often needs a **pump** that brings air into the water.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bony arch on which the gill filaments sit.
A hard flap that protects the gills in bony fish.
A gas that living things need for breathing.
Water and blood flow in opposite directions, so more oxygen is taken up.

gewusst: A litre of water contains about thirty times less oxygen than a litre of air.
Spread out, the gills of a fish would have a much larger area than its whole body.

teile.einleitung: Damselflies are delicate dragonflies with a thin, rod-shaped body. In summer you often see them at ponds, streams and lake shores, where they whirr over the water like small coloured needles. Typical of them is that at rest they fold their wings back together over the abdomen.
wichtigste: Damselflies are one of the two big groups of dragonflies; the other is the true dragonflies.
Most damselflies hold their wings folded back over the abdomen at rest.
Their four wings are almost the same shape.
Their eyes are set far apart on the sides of the head.
The larvae live in water and breathe with three leaf-like gills at the rear end.
Damselflies are predators and catch small insects in flight.
Well-known species in Switzerland are the demoiselles, the azure damselflies and the white-legged damselfly.

abschnitte.text: Damselflies have a very slender, long abdomen, often bright blue, green, red or metallic and shiny. Their four **wings** are about the same size and narrow at the base. The two **compound eyes** sit far apart, so that the head looks like a hammer. In the true dragonflies, by contrast, the eyes often touch in the middle.

When a damselfly is perched, it usually folds its wings back together over the abdomen. True dragonflies, by contrast, hold their wings spread out to the sides at rest. An exception are the **spreadwings**, which hold their wings half open. Damselflies fly more slowly and flutteringly than the large, powerful species.

The females usually lay their eggs in plant stems in or near the water. From them hatch **larvae** that live in the water for months or up to two years. At the rear end they have three leaf-like gill plates with which they breathe. Finally they climb out of the water on a stalk, and the finished dragonfly emerges from the larval skin.

Damselflies and their larvae are **predators**. The adults catch small flying insects such as midges and aphids, often in flight or from plants. The larvae catch small animals in the water with a fold-out lower lip, the **mask**. They themselves are eaten by birds, fish, frogs and larger dragonflies.

When mating, the male holds the female by the abdomen with claspers. The female bends her abdomen forwards, and so the typical **mating wheel** is formed, which often looks like a heart. In many species the pair stays together as a tandem while the eggs are laid. That way the male can prevent other males from mating with the female.

Several dozen species of damselfly live in Swiss waters. Often seen is the **azure damselfly**, which has a blue and black pattern. At streams, the banded demoiselle and the beautiful demoiselle stand out with their dark-coloured wings. Because many species need clean water, some are threatened by the disappearance of wetlands.

begriffe.erklaerung: The other large group of dragonflies, with a powerful body and wings spread out at rest.
An eye made of many thousands of tiny single eyes, typical of insects.
The fold-out lower lip of the dragonfly larva with which it seizes prey.
The heart-shaped position of male and female when mating.

gewusst: Dragonflies existed over 300 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs.
Dragonflies can neither sting nor bite; they are completely harmless to people.

teile.einleitung: Lanolin is a natural fat that sheep make in their skin and give off to their wool. That is why freshly shorn sheep’s wool usually feels a little greasy and soft. People have used this wool grease for a long time for ointments, creams and lip care.
wichtigste: Lanolin is a waxy fat from the wool of sheep.
It is made by sebaceous glands in the skin of the sheep.
Freshly shorn wool therefore feels a little greasy and soft.
The fat protects the wool and skin of the sheep from rain and drying out.
Lanolin is obtained when washing the shorn raw wool.
It is in many creams, ointments and lip balms.
Some people react allergically to wool wax.

abschnitte.text: Lanolin is a fat, more exactly a wax, that sheep make themselves. It arises in the **sebaceous glands** of the skin and lies like a thin film around every wool hair. In German it is also called **Wollwachs** (wool wax) or Wollfett (wool grease). The name lanolin comes from Latin: ‘lana’ means wool and ‘oleum’ means oil.

For the sheep the wool grease is a kind of natural raincoat. It makes the wool **water-repellent**, so that rain tends to bead off and the animal does not get wet to the skin. It also keeps skin and hair supple and protects them from wind and cold. That is why wet sheep smell so typically of wool and fat.

After **shearing**, the raw wool is full of fat, dirt and plant remains. Before it can be spun, it is washed with warm water and detergents. In the process the fat dissolves, and the lanolin is separated from the wash water and purified. So no sheep has to suffer for lanolin, it arises in wool processing.

Lanolin can bind a lot of water and makes the skin soft. That is why it is in many **ointments**, hand creams, lip balms and baby creams. It is also used for caring for leather, as rust protection and in wool detergents. From lanolin people also obtain a starting material for making **vitamin D3**.

Not everybody tolerates lanolin well. Some people get a **contact allergy** from it, with itchy, reddened skin. On packaging it often appears under the name ‘lanolin’ or ‘wool wax’. Anyone who is sensitive should read the list of ingredients closely.

In Switzerland there are several hundred thousand sheep, for example White Alpine sheep or Valais Blacknose sheep. They are usually sheared once or twice a year. Anyone who has ever touched freshly shorn wool knows the greasy feeling on the hands. Afterwards, by the way, the hands are often especially soft.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small gland in the skin that makes fat.
Another word for lanolin, the fat from sheep’s wool.
Wool straight after shearing, still unwashed.
A skin reaction when you touch something the body does not tolerate.

gewusst: Unwashed sheep’s wool can consist to a large extent of fat and dirt.
In the past sailors rubbed wool grease into their hands to protect them from salt water.
Socks made of unwashed wool keep feet drier thanks to the fat.

teile.einleitung: Dragonflies are fast and skilful flyers that you often see at ponds and streams in summer. They are insects and a very old animal group, whose ancestors lived over 300 million years ago. They spend their youth as larvae under water.
wichtigste: Dragonflies are insects and form the order Odonata.
Wings and legs sit on the thorax.
Large dragonflies fly as fast as about 50 kilometres per hour.
The larvae live in water, often for one to several years.
Adult dragonflies here usually live a few weeks to a few months.
Here most dragonflies fly from spring to autumn, above all in summer.
Dragonflies are harmless to people, they do not sting.

abschnitte.text: Dragonflies are **insects** and, like all insects, have a head, thorax and abdomen. On the head sit two huge **compound eyes** made of thousands of single eyes, with which they can see almost all round. On the thorax sit the six legs and the four wings, which they can move independently of each other. The long, slender abdomen is often coloured bright blue, red or green.

Dragonflies can hover in the air, fly backwards and change direction in a flash. Large species reach about 50 kilometres per hour. Their prey, such as midges and flies, they catch in flight with their legs, which they form into a basket. A distinction is made between **damselflies**, which fold their wings together at rest, and dragonflies proper, which hold them spread out.

Many females lay their eggs in the water or in water plants. Some have an **ovipositor** for this, with which they pierce the eggs into plant stems. From the eggs hatch larvae that, depending on the species, live one to several years in the water and hunt tadpoles, insect larvae or small fish. For this they have a **mask**, a lower lip that they shoot forward in a flash.

When the larva is fully grown, it climbs out of the water on a plant stem. Its skin splits open on the back, and the finished dragonfly squeezes out, with no pupal stage in between. Afterwards it pumps up its wings and lets them dry. The empty larval skin, the **exuvia**, often stays hanging on the stem.

The ancestors of dragonflies were already flying over 300 million years ago, long before the dinosaurs. The giant dragonfly **Meganeura** had a wingspan of about 70 centimetres. Today over 6,000 species are known worldwide, in Switzerland about 75. In old German names such as Azurjungfer or Mosaikjungfer, ‘Jungfer’ (maiden) simply stands for dragonfly.

Many species of dragonfly are threatened because pools, bogs and near-natural streams have disappeared. The best way to help them is with a near-natural **garden pond** without fish, because fish eat the larvae. In Japan dragonflies are traditionally regarded as a symbol of courage and victory. Because they need clean waters, dragonflies also show how healthy a water is.

begriffe.erklaerung: An eye made of many small single eyes, typical of insects.
The juvenile form of an animal that looks different from the adult.
The extendable lower lip of the dragonfly larva for catching prey.
The empty skin left behind after hatching.
The scientific name of dragonflies.

gewusst: Dragonflies catch the great majority of the animals they go for, far more often than lions, for example.
A dragonfly can steer each of its four wings separately.
The giant dragonflies of prehistoric times were as big as today’s pigeons.

teile.einleitung: Cranes are large, long-legged birds with a long neck, known for their loud trumpeting calls and their dances. In Europe it is mainly the common crane that lives. In autumn and spring tens of thousands of them travel across the sky in impressive formations.
wichtigste: There are 15 species of crane worldwide.
In Europe the common crane breeds, and it is about 1.2 metres tall.
Its wingspan is about two metres.
On migration, cranes often fly in a V formation.
Cranes call loudly with a trumpeting sound, and you can hear them for kilometres.
In courtship the pairs dance with leaps and wing flapping.
In Japan cranes are regarded as a symbol of good luck and a sign of long life.

abschnitte.text: The **common crane** has grey plumage, a black and white neck and a red patch on the head. It stands on long, dark legs and is about 1.2 metres tall. With its wings spread it measures about two metres. In flight it stretches neck and legs straight out, which distinguishes it from the grey heron, which pulls its neck in.

Common cranes breed in bogs, marshes and damp woods in northern and eastern Europe, for example in Scandinavia, Poland and northern Germany. In autumn they travel south-west, and many spend the winter in France and Spain. On the way they stop at **resting places**, where sometimes tens of thousands of birds gather. In the **V formation** each bird saves energy because it flies in the updraft of the bird ahead.

Cranes are omnivores. They eat grains, seeds, roots and tubers, but also insects, worms, snails, frogs and small mice. On harvested fields in autumn they look for maize left lying. With their long beak they probe in the soft ground.

Cranes often stay with the same partner for life. In **courtship** they leap into the air, bow and throw up tufts of grass. The pair calls together in a duet as they do so. Usually the female lays two eggs in a nest on the ground, and both parents incubate for about a month.

No cranes breed in Switzerland. But you can watch them in autumn and spring, when they fly across the country on migration. With a little luck you can hear their trumpeting calls high in the sky. In central Europe the populations have increased again in recent decades thanks to bog protection.

begriffe.erklaerung: The wooing of a partner before mating.
A place where migrating birds rest and feed on the way.
A flight arrangement in the shape of the letter V that saves energy in flight.
A bird that flies back and forth every year between its breeding area and its wintering area.

gewusst: In Japan people fold 1,000 paper cranes, because according to an old legend that is supposed to grant a wish.
The windpipe of the crane is coiled and very long, which is why its calls sound like a trumpet.

teile.einleitung: The adder, or common European viper, is a venomous snake that also occurs in Switzerland. It is easy to recognise by the dark zigzag band on its back. Although it is venomous, it is shy and bites only when it feels threatened.
wichtigste: The adder belongs to the vipers and is venomous.
Its body is stocky and relatively short, usually 50 to 70 centimetres long.
On its back it has a dark zigzag band.
Males are often grey, females more brown in colour.
It kills its prey, above all mice, with a venomous bite.
In Switzerland it lives mainly in the Alps and the Jura.
Because its habitat is disappearing, it is threatened and protected in Switzerland.
The females give birth to about 5 to 15 live young.

abschnitte.text: The adder has a stocky, relatively short body with a short tail. Its head is clearly set off from the neck and bears a dark marking on the crown, often in the shape of an X or V. Typical is the **zigzag band** on the back. Males are often grey with a black pattern, females more brown. There are also entirely black animals, which are called **black adders**.

The adder is the snake with the largest range in the world, extending from western Europe to the Pacific coast of Asia. It even lives north of the Arctic Circle. In Switzerland it is found mainly in the Alps and the Jura, often high up on mountain pastures, in bogs and at woodland edges. As hiding places it uses piles of stones, stacks of wood and dense dwarf shrubs.

The adder eats mainly mice, but also lizards and frogs. It kills its prey with a **venomous bite** and then follows it until the venom takes effect. It detects smells with its forked tongue, which carries scent particles to a smelling organ in the roof of the mouth. Because it eats many mice, it helps to regulate their numbers.

After **hibernation** in a frost-free hiding place, adders come out in spring. Then it is mating season, and the males sometimes fight in a wrestling match over the females. In late summer the female gives birth to about 5 to 15 young, which are independent right after birth. The eggs develop inside the mother’s body, which is an advantage in cold regions.

In Switzerland the adder is threatened because its habitat is disappearing through buildings, roads and intensive farming. Like all native reptiles, it is legally **protected**. When hiking it is advisable to wear sturdy footwear and not to reach blindly into grass or under stones. A bite is painful and must be treated in hospital, but is only very rarely life-threatening for healthy people.

begriffe.erklaerung: A family of venomous snakes with long, movable fangs.
A resting state in winter in which the animal uses hardly any energy.
An adder that is coloured entirely black.
Cold-blooded animals with scaly skin, for example snakes and lizards.

gewusst: The adder lives further north than any other snake in the world.
Black adders warm up in the sun faster than light-coloured ones, which is handy in the mountains.

teile.einleitung: After the emperor penguin, the king penguin is the second largest penguin species in the world. The bright orange-yellow feathers on its head are reminiscent of a crown. It lives on islands in the Southern Ocean and is an excellent diver.
wichtigste: The king penguin is called Aptenodytes patagonicus in science.
It grows to about 90 centimetres tall and is thus the second largest penguin species.
Typical are orange-yellow patches on the head, neck and chest.
It breeds on sub-Antarctic islands, for example on South Georgia.
King penguins do not build a nest, and the egg lies on the parents’ feet.
They eat mainly small fish and squid.
You can watch king penguins at Zurich Zoo.

abschnitte.text: A king penguin grows to about 90 centimetres tall and usually weighs 10 to 16 kilograms. Back and head are dark, the belly is white. Striking are the **orange-yellow ear patches** and the orange colouring on the chest and beak. Its dense, multi-layered **plumage** and a layer of fat protect it from the cold water.

King penguins live on **sub-Antarctic islands** such as South Georgia, the Crozet Islands, the Kerguelen Islands, Macquarie Island and the Falkland Islands. There they form huge breeding colonies, often of tens of thousands of animals. Unlike the emperor penguin, they do not breed on the ice of Antarctica. To hunt, they swim far out into the open sea.

King penguins eat mainly small **lanternfish** and squid. They usually dive over 100 metres deep, sometimes even over 300 metres. Under water they move along with their wings like paddles. Their wings have become stiff flippers, and they cannot fly.

The female lays a single egg, which the parents incubate on their feet under a warm **brood pouch**. Male and female take turns at this while the other partner feeds in the sea. After about 54 days the chick hatches, wearing a thick, brown coat of down. Because raising a chick takes over a year, a pair raises at most two young in three years.

In the 19th century king penguins were killed in huge numbers to obtain oil from their fat. Since they have been protected, many colonies have recovered well. Today they are considered not threatened. **Climate change** could, however, shift their feeding grounds further south and make the search for food harder.

At **Zurich Zoo** king penguins live together with other penguin species. In winter, in cold weather, there is the popular penguin walk through the zoo. The animals waddle along ahead of the visitors of their own accord. Such walks give the penguins exercise and variety.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large group of animals of one species that breed together.
A sea and island region north of Antarctica with a cool climate.
A fold of skin on the belly that keeps an egg or chick warm.
Soft, fluffy feathers that keep especially warm.

gewusst: The brown, fluffy chicks are often larger and heavier than their parents and were once thought to be a penguin species of their own.
Parents and chicks find each other in the noisy colony by their unmistakable calls.
A king penguin can hold its breath under water for several minutes.

teile.einleitung: Spawn is the name for the eggs of fish, frogs, toads and other water animals. They are usually released into the water and fertilised there. When fish release their eggs into the water, they are said to spawn.
wichtigste: Spawn is the eggs of fish and amphibians.
When fish release their eggs into the water, this is called spawning.
The eggs are usually only fertilised by the male in the water.
Frogspawn forms clumps, toadspawn long strings.
Fish spawn is called roe in the kitchen, and in sturgeon caviar.
Many fish lay thousands or even millions of eggs.
The time in which animals spawn is called the spawning season.

abschnitte.text: **Spawn** is the eggs of animals that reproduce in water, above all fish and amphibians. The eggs have no hard shell like birds’ eggs, but a soft covering. They are often surrounded by a transparent jelly that protects them. Snails and some mussels also lay spawn.

In **spawning** the female releases her eggs into the water, and the male releases his sperm fluid, the milt, over them. In this way the eggs are fertilised outside the body. Some fish let their eggs drift freely in the water, others stick them to plants or stones. Trout and salmon bury their eggs in a spawning pit in the gravel.

In spring you often see large clumps of transparent balls with black dots in ponds, which is **frogspawn**. Toads, by contrast, lay their spawn in long strings that they wind around water plants. From each egg a tadpole hatches after a few days to weeks. You should not take spawn home from the wild, because amphibians are protected.

Most fish do not look after their eggs, so they lay a great many of them. A pike lays tens of thousands of eggs, a cod even several million. Only a tiny part of them become adult fish, as many eggs and larvae are eaten. Fish that guard their brood, such as the stickleback, lay far fewer eggs.

Every species has its own **spawning season**. Pike and common frogs spawn in early spring, whitefish and trout, by contrast, in autumn and winter. In this time **closed seasons** apply in Switzerland for many fish, in which they may not be caught. In this way they can reproduce undisturbed.

begriffe.erklaerung: The eggs of fish when they are used as food.
The salted roe of sturgeons, an expensive delicacy.
A time of year in which a species of animal may not be caught or hunted.
A transparent, slimy mass that protects eggs.

gewusst: Frogspawn first sinks and then rises to the surface, where the sun warms the eggs.
Some fish such as the salmon return to spawn at exactly the place where they themselves hatched.

teile.einleitung: Octopuses are sea animals with eight arms, a soft body without bones and a surprisingly clever brain. They can change colour in a flash and squeeze through tiny gaps. Their German name, Krake, recalls old stories about a gigantic sea monster.
wichtigste: Octopuses are cephalopods and belong to the molluscs.
There are about 300 species of octopus worldwide, and all live in the sea.
Because octopuses have no bones, they fit through very narrow gaps.
Unlike the squid, the octopus has no two long tentacles, but eight arms of the same kind.
Uncamouflaged, octopuses are usually brownish grey.
Most octopuses live only one to two years.
The female guards her eggs, eats almost nothing in the process and dies soon after the young hatch.

abschnitte.text: An octopus has a sack-like body, the **mantle**, and eight arms with suckers. It has no bones, only the beak in its mouth is hard. That is why it can squeeze through any opening that is larger than its beak. The smallest octopus is only a few centimetres across, while the **giant Pacific octopus** can measure several metres with its arms outstretched.

Octopuses live in all seas, from shallow coasts to the **deep sea**. Many hide by day in rock crevices, caves or even in empty mussel shells. In the Mediterranean the common octopus is widespread. Octopuses breathe with gills and so need the oxygen from the water.

Octopuses hunt mainly crustaceans, crabs, mussels and fish. With their suckers they can also taste and feel. They open mussels by force or drill a hole in the shell with their rasping tongue. A **venom** in the saliva paralyses the prey.

Octopuses are regarded as the most intelligent invertebrates. In experiments they opened screw-top jars and found their way through mazes. In their skin there are colour cells with which they change colour and pattern in fractions of a second in order to **camouflage** themselves. When in danger they release a cloud of ink, although they themselves can hardly hear anything.

The female lays thousands of small eggs in a cave and hangs them in clusters from the ceiling. For weeks or months she guards and cleans the eggs and fans fresh water over them. During this time she eats almost nothing. Shortly after the young have hatched, the female dies, which is why octopuses usually live only **one to two years**.

The German name Krake probably comes from old Norse tales about the **kraken**, a gigantic sea monster that dragged ships down into the depths. Behind such stories there may be sightings of giant squid. Today the octopus fascinates many people with its cleverness. In Swiss zoos and aquariums you can sometimes watch octopuses, but they do not occur in lakes.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal group in which the arms sit directly on the head.
The sack-like part of an octopus’s body in which the organs lie.
An adhesive disc on the arms for holding on and feeling.
Adapting to the surroundings so as not to be seen.

gewusst: An octopus has three hearts and blue blood.
A large part of an octopus’s nerve cells sits not in its head but in its arms.
The blue-ringed octopus is hardly bigger than a golf ball, but one of the most poisonous sea animals.

teile.einleitung: The leatherback turtle is the largest turtle in the world and a true giant of the oceans. Unlike other sea turtles it has no hard shell, but one that feels soft like leather. It likes best to eat jellyfish.
wichtigste: The leatherback is the largest sea turtle and the largest turtle of all.
Its shell is covered with a leathery skin instead of hard plates.
Large animals weigh several hundred kilograms.
It feeds mainly on jellyfish.
It dives deeper than any other turtle.
It swims through all the oceans, even into cool waters.
The species is threatened, among other things by plastic waste in the sea.

abschnitte.text: The leatherback usually grows to about 1.5 to 1.8 metres long and often weighs 300 to 500 kilograms. The heaviest known animal, found in Wales in 1988, weighed over 900 kilograms. Its back shell consists of many small bony plates under a thick, **leathery skin**. On it run seven lengthwise ridges that look like grooves, and the skin is dark with pale patches.

Leatherbacks eat almost only **jellyfish** and other jelly-like sea animals such as pyrosomes. Since jellyfish consist almost only of water, the turtle has to eat huge amounts of them. In its throat it has many sharp, backward-pointing spikes so that the slippery prey does not slide out again. Its sharp jaw edges cut the jellyfish into pieces as it does so.

The leatherback lives in all oceans, from the tropics to cool waters off Canada or Norway. That it can stand the cold is due to its size and a thick layer of fat that stores body heat. Every year it travels thousands of kilometres between feeding grounds and nesting sites. When diving it reaches depths of over 1,000 metres.

To lay eggs, the females crawl at night onto tropical **sandy beaches**, for example in West Africa, Central America or South-East Asia. With their hind flippers they dig a hole and lay about 80 to 100 eggs in it. They repeat this several times in a season. After about two months the young hatch and run straight to the sea, and the **sand temperature** decides whether more males or females result.

Many leatherbacks mistake floating **plastic bags** for jellyfish and swallow them, which can be fatal. They also get caught in fishing nets and long lines. On some beaches eggs are collected or the nesting sites are disturbed by buildings and light. That is why the species is on the Red List and is protected in many countries.

On many beaches conservationists and volunteers guard the nests and help the young. Less plastic in everyday life also helps the turtles, because a lot of rubbish ends up in the sea via rivers. This applies even to Switzerland, because the Rhine flows all the way to the North Sea. Leatherbacks are the last living representatives of a very old group of turtles.

begriffe.erklaerung: The hard protective covering of turtles, covered with skin in the leatherback.
A raised strip that runs lengthwise over the shell.
A list of threatened species of animals and plants.
A place where animals lay their eggs.

gewusst: Leatherbacks can keep their body temperature clearly above that of the surrounding water.
The leatherback has existed in almost unchanged form for millions of years.
The leatherback is the only living species of its family.

teile.einleitung: Cats do not speak with words, but they communicate in many ways: with sounds, with their bodies and with smells. Anyone who understands cat language soon notices whether a cat is content, frightened or annoyed. That way you can handle it better and avoid misunderstandings.
wichtigste: Cats communicate with sounds, body language and scents.
Cats use meowing mainly to communicate with people.
Purring often means well-being, but sometimes also stress or pain.
A tail held high is a friendly greeting.
If the tail swishes quickly back and forth, the cat is irritated or nervous.
Ears turned backwards often show fear or anger.
Slow blinking is a sign of trust.

abschnitte.text: Cats have many different sounds. Adult cats hardly **meow** at each other; they use meowing mainly to speak to people. **Hissing** and growling are clear warnings that say: stay away! When a cat sees a bird at the window, it often makes a soft, excited chattering.

**Purring** is a deep, even rumble that is produced in the larynx. Cats usually purr when they feel comfortable, for example when being stroked. Sometimes, however, they also purr when they are ill, injured or stressed, probably to calm themselves. Even kittens purr when feeding from their mother.

The tail is like a mood indicator. A tail held high means a friendly **greeting**. If the tail swishes quickly back and forth, the cat is irritated or nervous, and then it is better to leave it in peace. A fluffed-up tail shows great fright or fear.

Ears pointing forwards show curiosity and attention. Ears turned backwards or laid flat often show fear or anger. Very large **pupils** can mean excitement, playfulness or fear. An arched back with bristling fur is meant to make the cat look bigger and more dangerous.

Cats have **scent glands** on the cheeks, chin, paws and at the base of the tail. When a cat rubs its head against people or furniture, it marks them with its scent as familiar. When scratching trees, too, it leaves scent and visible marks. It is mainly un-neutered tomcats that mark their territory with urine.

If a cat slowly blinks at you, you can blink back just as slowly; this shows trust. **Kneading** with the front paws on a soft blanket shows that the cat feels secure. If a cat shows its belly, it is a sign of trust, but not always an invitation to stroke it. Always watch for warning signs such as hissing or a lashing tail.

begriffe.erklaerung: A cat’s hissing warning sound.
Pressing alternately with the front paws, also called making biscuits.
Communication through posture, movements and facial expression.
A smell that an animal leaves behind to mark something.

gewusst: Cats have learned that meowing works on people, which is why domestic cats meow much more than wild cats.
Some cats mix a high tone into their purr that sounds a little like a crying baby and gets people to feed them.

teile.einleitung: Corals look like colourful stones or plants, but they are animals. Many tiny coral polyps together build huge coral reefs, which are among the most species-rich habitats on Earth. Tiny algae that live in their bodies help them to do so.
wichtigste: Corals belong to the animal phylum of cnidarians (Cnidaria) and to the class Anthozoa.
The reef-building stony corals form the order Scleractinia.
Their skeleton consists of aragonite, a form of calcium carbonate.
A coral polyp has only a single opening for taking in food and excreting waste.
With stinging cells on the tentacles, polyps catch small prey from the plankton.
In many corals live zooxanthellae, single-celled algae from the group of dinoflagellates.
In coral bleaching the coral expels its zooxanthellae and turns white.

abschnitte.text: A coral consists of many small **polyps**, which look like tiny sea anemones. Each polyp has a tube-shaped body with a ring of tentacles around the mouth opening. In stony corals, tentacles and inner partitions are arranged in **sixes**. Many polyps are joined together and form a **colony** that grows together.

Stony corals secrete a hard skeleton of **aragonite**, a form of limestone, beneath them. When a polyp dies, the skeleton remains, and new polyps grow on it. In this way huge coral reefs arise over thousands of years. The largest is the **Great Barrier Reef** off Australia, which is over 2,000 kilometres long.

At night many polyps stretch out their tentacles and use **stinging cells** to catch tiny animals from the plankton. The food goes in through the single body opening, and leftovers are excreted through the same opening again. Reef-building corals get most of their energy, however, from their lodgers. Up to about 90 per cent of their energy needs are supplied to them by the zooxanthellae.

The **zooxanthellae** are single-celled dinoflagellates that live in the tissue of the polyps. They carry out photosynthesis and give sugar to the coral. In return they receive protection, carbon dioxide and nutrients. Because the algae need light, reef-building corals grow only in clear, shallow, warm sea water in the tropics. Such a partnership for mutual benefit is called **symbiosis**.

If the water becomes too warm, the coral expels its zooxanthellae. You can then see the white limestone skeleton through the colourless tissue, which is called **coral bleaching**. If the heat lasts too long, the coral starves and dies. Because of climate change, major bleaching events are happening more and more often, and pollution, overfishing and the acidification of the oceans do further harm.

There were once coral reefs in the area of present-day Switzerland too. About 150 million years ago there was a warm, shallow sea here in which corals grew. Their traces can be found today as **fossils** in the limestone of the Jura. Reefs are important because they protect coasts from waves and provide a habitat for a large part of all sea animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small, tube-shaped animal with tentacles, the basic building block of a coral.
Tiny algae that live in corals and supply them with food.
Two living things living together for mutual benefit.
The fading of corals when they lose their algae.
Tiny living things that float in the water.

gewusst: The Great Barrier Reef is the largest structure built by living things on Earth and can be seen from space.
Many corals of a reef release eggs and sperm into the water at the same time on the same night.
There are also cold-water corals that live without light in the deep sea, for example off Norway.

teile.einleitung: The cuckoo clock is a wall clock in which, every hour, a little wooden bird springs out of a small door and calls ‘cuck-oo’. It gets its name from this figure, which calls like a cuckoo. It comes from the Black Forest in southern Germany and is a popular souvenir worldwide.
wichtigste: The cuckoo clock became known in the Black Forest in the 18th century.
On every full hour the cuckoo calls as many times as the hour.
The call is produced by two small bellows with pipes.
The clock is usually driven by weights in the shape of pine cones.
Typical are carvings with leaves, birds and animals.
Many tourists think it is Swiss, although it comes from Germany.

abschnitte.text: A cuckoo clock is a mechanical **pendulum clock** that hangs on the wall. Above the dial there is a little door from which a small cuckoo hops on the full hour. It calls as many times as the hour, so three times at three o’clock. On many clocks it calls once at the half hour.

The clock is driven by **weights**, which often look like pine cones and hang on chains. A pendulum makes sure the clock ticks evenly. The call is produced by two small **bellows**, which push air through two pipes with different notes. You have to pull the weights up regularly, daily or once a week depending on the movement.

The cuckoo clock became known in the 18th century in the **Black Forest** in southern Germany, where many farmers built clocks in winter. Traders carried the clocks on their backs all over Europe. Around 1850 the shape of the ‘Bahnhäusle’ (railway cottage) arose in a competition at the clockmaking school in Furtwangen. This case looks like a little signalman’s house on a railway line.

The best-known style is the **hunting style** with carved leaves, birds, stag heads or hares. Other clocks look like chalets with dancing figures, mill wheels and musical movements. Many cases are still carved by hand from lime wood today. There are also modern cuckoo clocks in plain, colourful shapes.

Many people in the world associate the cuckoo clock with Switzerland. In Swiss souvenir shops, for example in Lucerne or Interlaken, they are often sold. The cuckoo clock was not invented in Switzerland, however, but in the neighbouring Black Forest. The mistake probably comes from the fact that both regions are known for mountains, wooden houses and clocks.

begriffe.erklaerung: A swinging weight that sets the even beat of a clock.
A small bag that presses air out when squeezed.
The inner workings of a clock made of gear wheels and springs or weights.
A keepsake that you bring back from a trip.

gewusst: In the Black Forest two places argue over which has the largest cuckoo clock in the world.
The cuckoo call of the clock consists of two notes, like the call of the real cuckoo.

teile.einleitung: Dogs speak with their whole body. With tail, ears, eyes, mouth and posture they show whether they feel cheerful, afraid, unsure or threatening. Anyone who understands this body language can meet dogs more safely and respectfully.
wichtigste: Dogs communicate mainly through body language, smells and sounds.
A tightly tucked tail usually means fear or submission.
Tail wagging does not always mean joy, but first of all excitement.
The play bow, in which the dog goes down on its front legs, is an invitation to play.
Yawning, licking and looking away can be signs of stress or appeasement.
Bared teeth, growling and a stiff body are clear warning signals.
Children should only touch a strange dog if the owner allows it.

abschnitte.text: Dogs descend from the wolf and live in social groups. To avoid quarrels they have developed a fine **body language**. They show their mood through posture, movements and facial expression. Added to this are sounds such as barking, growling or whining, as well as many scent signals.

A loosely wagging tail at medium height often shows joy and friendliness. A tail carried high and stiff can mean self-confidence or tension. A tail held low or **tucked** between the hind legs usually shows fear or submission. It is important to look not only at the tail, but always at the whole dog.

Ears pointing forward show attention, ears laid flat rather uncertainty or fear. A relaxed dog has a slightly open mouth and soft eyes. If a lot of white can be seen in the eye, the so-called **whale eye**, the dog often feels uncomfortable. A long, fixed stare can be a threat.

In the **play bow** the dog lowers its front legs, stretches its rear end up and wags. In this way it says: ‘Everything that happens now is play.’ With **appeasement signals** such as yawning, licking the nose, turning the head away or sniffing the ground, dogs try to calm a tense situation. They show them towards other dogs and towards people too.

Before a dog bites, it usually warns clearly. It freezes, stares, pulls up its lips, bares its teeth or **growls**. Sometimes the hair on the back also stands up, which is called hackles. You should never punish growling, because it is an important warning that prevents bites.

Always ask the owner first before you stroke a strange dog. Let the dog sniff your hand instead of reaching over its head, and stroke it rather at the side of the neck or on the chest. Never disturb dogs when they are eating, sleeping or retreating. If a dog runs towards you, stand still and calm like a **tree**, look away and fold your arms.

begriffe.erklaerung: Communication through posture, movement and facial expression.
Behaviour with which a dog wants to calm a situation.
A typical posture with which a dog invites play.
The lips of the dog.

gewusst: According to studies, dogs wag more to the right when they see something pleasant, and more to the left at something unpleasant.
A dog that shows you its belly does not always want to be tickled, sometimes it is simply unsure.
Dogs pay very close attention to our body language and often recognise whether we are cheerful or tense.

teile.einleitung: Gills are the breathing organs of fish and many other water animals. With them the animals take oxygen directly from the water. That is how a perch in a lake can breathe without ever coming to the surface.
wichtigste: Gills take oxygen from the water and give off carbon dioxide.
Fish such as the perch, the whitefish and sharks breathe with gills.
Gills consist of many very thin gill filaments rich in blood vessels.
In bony fish a hard gill cover protects the gills.
Most sharks have five open gill slits on each side.
Gill rakers filter food from the water in fish such as whitefish.
Tadpoles, crustaceans, mussels and many insect larvae also breathe with gills.

abschnitte.text: Gills are organs with which animals breathe in water. In fish they sit behind the head, on the left and right. Water contains much less oxygen than air. That is why gills have to be very good at extracting the dissolved **oxygen**.

In fish the gills sit on curved bony bars, the **gill arches**. From them hang hundreds of fine **gill filaments**, which lie close together like the pages of a book. Their walls are wafer-thin and full of tiny blood vessels. Because so much blood flows through, healthy gills look bright red.

The fish takes in water through its mouth and presses it out again over the gills. In the process oxygen passes from the water into the blood, and carbon dioxide passes into the water. In the gill filaments the blood flows in exactly the opposite direction to the water, which is called the **counter-current principle**. This lets the fish take up an especially large amount of oxygen.

Bony fish such as the perch or the trout have a movable **gill cover** that protects the gills and helps with pumping. Sharks and rays have no cover, but open **gill slits**, usually five on each side. Some sharks have to keep swimming so that enough water flows over their gills. Other sharks can also pump water through their gills while lying on the bottom.

On the inner side of the gill arches, many fish have small projections called **gill rakers**. They hold back food and protect the delicate gill filaments. The whitefish in Swiss lakes have especially long and dense rakers. With them they filter tiny plankton such as water fleas from the water.

It is not only fish that have gills. Tadpoles breathe with gills until they turn into frogs with lungs. The Mexican axolotl even keeps its frilly **external gills** for its whole life. Crustaceans, mussels, squid and the larvae of many insects such as dragonflies also have gills.

begriffe.erklaerung: A thin, blood-rich plate of the gills through which oxygen enters the blood.
A hard bony plate that covers and protects the gills in bony fish.
Small projections on the gill arches that hold back food like a sieve.
Blood and water flow in opposite directions so that more oxygen gets into the blood.

gewusst: On land the fine gill filaments collapse and stick together, which is why a fish out of water suffocates despite all the air.
Fishermen and cooks recognise a fresh fish partly by its bright red gills.

teile.einleitung: Coprophagy means ‘eating dung’. Animals that feed wholly or partly on dung are called coprophages. What sounds disgusting to us is very useful in nature, because these animals tidy up and bring nutrients back into the soil.
wichtigste: Coprophagy literally means ‘eating dung’, and the word comes from Greek.
Animals that feed on dung are called coprophages.
Well-known coprophages are dung beetles, scarab beetles and many fly larvae.
Rabbits and hares eat a special, soft kind of dropping straight again.
Young koalas and elephants eat their mother’s dung to get useful gut bacteria.
Coprophages help to break down dung and fertilise the soil as they do so.
Dogs also sometimes eat dung, which is usually harmless but unwanted.

abschnitte.text: The term is made up of the Greek words ‘kopros’ for dung and ‘phagein’ for eating. Dung often still contains many **nutrients**, because animals do not digest their food completely. Herbivores in particular, such as cows or horses, excrete a lot of undigested plant material. Other animals use this as a source of food.

The best-known **coprophages** are beetles. The **scarab beetle** forms a ball from dung and rolls it away to lay eggs in it. Other dung beetles dig tunnels under cowpats and carry dung deep into the soil. In Switzerland there are numerous species of dung beetle, for example on alpine pastures.

Rabbits and hares produce two kinds of dropping. Besides the familiar hard pellets there is soft **caecotrope**, which they take up again directly from the anus. It contains vitamins and proteins that bacteria in the caecum have made. Only on the second pass through the gut can they absorb these substances.

Young **koalas** eat a special paste from their mother’s dung. In this way bacteria reach their gut that they need in order to digest poisonous eucalyptus leaves later. Young elephants, hippopotamuses and horses also sometimes eat the dung of adult animals. In this way they build up their **gut flora**.

Without coprophages, cowpats and other droppings would lie around much longer. The animals break the dung up, mix it into the soil and so turn it into **fertiliser**. At the same time they take away breeding places from flies and parasites. In Australia, dung beetles from other continents were therefore even introduced to break down cattle dung.

Some dogs eat the dung of cats, horses or other dogs. Mother dogs lick their puppies clean and eat their dung as they do so, which is quite normal. In adult dogs the behaviour can come from curiosity, boredom or hunger. Because **worms** and disease germs can be passed on this way, owners should stop it and ask the vet if it happens often.

begriffe.erklaerung: The eating of dung.
The droppings of animals, especially of large herbivores.
Soft, nutrient-rich droppings of rabbits that they eat again.
All the useful bacteria in the gut.

gewusst: A scarab beetle can roll a ball of dung that is much heavier than itself.
Some dung beetles find their way at night by the Milky Way in order to roll their ball in a straight line.
In ancient Egypt the scarab beetle was regarded as a sacred animal.

teile.einleitung: A cocoon is a firm covering that some animals build for themselves in order to spend an important phase of life in it, protected. Especially well known are the cocoons of moths, in which the caterpillar pupates. From the cocoon of the silkworm, people have obtained precious silk for thousands of years.
wichtigste: A cocoon is a protective covering that an animal usually builds from threads it has spun itself.
Many moth caterpillars pupate in a cocoon.
The thread for the cocoon comes from spinning glands on the caterpillar’s head.
In the cocoon the caterpillar turns into a butterfly by way of the pupa.
Silk is made from the cocoons of the silkworm.
Spiders, fleas and earthworms also form cocoons for themselves or their eggs.

abschnitte.text: A cocoon is a covering of threads, secretion or woven-in plant parts. It protects the animal from enemies, cold, wet and drying out. It is typical of insects with **complete metamorphosis**, that is, with the stages egg, larva, pupa and adult. The actual **pupa** lies inside the cocoon.

When the caterpillar is fully grown, it looks for a sheltered place, for example between leaves or in the ground. From **spinning glands** on its head it presses out a liquid that hardens in the air into a thread. In hours of work it moves its head back and forth in figures of eight and so wraps itself up. Some species also weave in hairs, bits of wood or soil.

In the cocoon the caterpillar moults one last time and becomes a pupa. After that its body is almost completely rebuilt: caterpillar legs and chewing mouthparts become wings, antennae and a sucking proboscis. This **metamorphosis** takes a few weeks or even a whole winter, depending on the species. To hatch, the moth often softens the cocoon with a liquid or cuts it open.

The **silkworm** is a moth whose caterpillars eat mulberry leaves. Its cocoon consists of a single, very long thread that can measure several hundred metres. To obtain silk, the cocoons are soaked in hot water and the thread is reeled off. Silk making comes from China, where for thousands of years it was a closely guarded secret.

It is not only caterpillars that build cocoons. Many spiders wrap their eggs in an **egg sac** of spider silk, which some females even carry around with them. Earthworms form small cocoons with their girdle, in which the young worms develop. Flea larvae and many wasps also pupate in a cocoon.

In Switzerland, silk processing was an important trade for a long time. In the 19th century Zurich was regarded as one of the most important silk cities of Europe, and in Basel silk ribbons were woven. In Ticino, silkworms were also bred in the past. In summer here you can also find the cocoons of native moths, for example on twigs or under tree bark.

begriffe.erklaerung: A protective covering that an animal builds from threads or other material.
The resting stage of an insect between larva and adult.
The change of an animal from one form into a completely different one.
A gland that makes a liquid from which a thread is formed.

gewusst: Day-flying butterflies usually do not build a cocoon; their pupae hang freely from twigs or stems.
The so-called ‘ant eggs’ you see in an anthill are in reality often cocoons with pupae inside.
For a single silk scarf you need the threads of many hundreds of cocoons.

teile.einleitung: The compost worm is a small, red earthworm that lives in compost heaps and manure. It eats rotting plant remains and turns them into nutrient-rich soil. That is why it is a hard-working helper for everyone who composts kitchen waste.
wichtigste: The compost worm is called Eisenia fetida in science and is also known as the manure worm.
It is smaller than the large lob worm and lives in rotting material instead of deep in the soil.
Typical are its red body and yellowish rings, which is why it is sometimes called the tiger worm.
It eats dead plant remains, manure and kitchen waste.
Valuable worm compost is made from its droppings.
Every compost worm is male and female at the same time.
It is used in worm bins, even on the balcony.

abschnitte.text: A compost worm usually grows to about 6 to 13 centimetres long. Its body is strongly red to reddish brown and has paler, yellowish rings between the segments. Like all earthworms it consists of many **segments** and has no eyes, but it senses light with its skin. If it is disturbed, it gives off a yellowish, strong-smelling liquid.

The compost worm lives where a lot of organic material is rotting, for example in compost heaps, leaf heaps and manure heaps. It stays near the surface and does not dig deep tunnels. In this it differs from the **lob worm**, which grows up to 30 centimetres long and digs deep, vertical tubes into the soil. Compost worms like it damp, warm and dark.

Compost worms eat dead plant parts, manure and kitchen waste such as vegetable and fruit remains. In doing so they actually eat mainly the **bacteria** and fungi that are already breaking the material down. In good conditions they can process about half their body weight every day. They tolerate meat, citrus peel in large amounts and salty things badly.

Every compost worm is a **hermaphrodite**, so it has both male and female sex organs. Even so, two worms always mate and exchange sperm. Afterwards the thickened band, the **clitellum**, forms a small cocoon in which several young worms develop. In good conditions compost worms multiply very quickly.

Compost worms turn waste into fertile soil, the so-called **worm compost**. It is rich in nutrients and well suited to garden beds and flower pots. In a worm bin you can compost in the flat or on the balcony without it smelling. Anglers also use compost worms as bait.

In Switzerland many families compost their garden waste themselves or put it in the green waste collection. In many municipalities there are also neighbourhood composts. In every healthy garden compost, compost worms usually turn up all by themselves. Worm bins with compost worms can be bought in garden centres or from specialist suppliers.

begriffe.erklaerung: Soil that is made from rotted plant remains.
A living thing that is male and female at the same time.
A thickened band on the worm’s body that forms the egg cocoon.
Dark, fertile soil made from decomposed plant and animal remains.

gewusst: The scientific name fetida means roughly ‘stinking’, because of the liquid the worm gives off when in danger.
Compost worms have no lungs, they breathe through their moist skin.
A worm bin can stand in a flat without an unpleasant smell if it is looked after properly.

teile.einleitung: The llama is a domestic animal from the Andes in South America and belongs to the camelids, but has no hump. For thousands of years llamas have carried loads and supplied wool, meat and dung. Today you can also see them in Switzerland on farms and on hikes.
wichtigste: Llamas belong to the New World camelids and come from South America.
Unlike dromedaries and Bactrian camels, they have no hump.
A llama can carry about a quarter of its body weight.
If the load is too heavy, it simply lies down.
Llamas are ruminants and chew their food a second time.
Bolivia is among the countries with especially many llamas.
Llama wool insulates well against cold and is a raw material for textiles.
Llamas often communicate with a soft humming.

abschnitte.text: A llama has a long neck, long legs and a dense, woolly coat in white, brown, black or spotted. It is about 1.1 to 1.3 metres tall at the shoulder and usually weighs 130 to 150 kilograms. Its ears are long and slightly curved inwards. On its feet it has two toes with soft **pads**, which spares the ground.

The llama was bred in the **Andes** several thousand years ago from the wild guanaco. Its relatives include the alpaca, the guanaco and the vicuña. Together they are called New World camelids, because they live in the Americas. Especially many llamas live today in Bolivia and Peru, where they live in the highlands at over 3,000 metres.

Llamas eat grass, hay, herbs and leaves. Like cows they are **ruminants**: after eating they bring the food up again and chew it once more so that it is digested better. In the upper jaw they have a hard dental pad at the front instead of a full row of incisors. Llamas need little water and manage with poor fodder.

Llamas live in herds and communicate with a soft **humming**. In quarrels they spit, but mostly at other llamas and rarely at people. After a gestation of about eleven months, one young is born, called a **cria**. Crias are usually born by day, often in the morning, so that they dry off before the cold night.

The Inca already used llamas as **pack animals** on their mountain paths. A llama carries about a quarter of its body weight, and if it gets too heavy, it lies down and goes on strike. Warm jumpers, hats and blankets are made from the wool, and the dung serves as fertiliser and fuel. In Switzerland llamas are kept for trekking tours and sometimes used as guard animals against foxes with sheep.

begriffe.erklaerung: The camelids of South America: llama, alpaca, guanaco and vicuña.
Animals that bring their food up again after eating and chew it once more.
The name for a young llama or alpaca.
A long high mountain range on the west coast of South America.

gewusst: Llamas deposit their dung in shared places, so the pasture stays clean.
In South America the llama is regarded as an important domestic animal and appears in many stories and festivals.

teile.einleitung: The salmon louse is a small crustacean that lives as a parasite on salmon and other salmonids. It feeds on the skin and blood of its hosts. Especially in large sea fish farms it multiplies strongly and so becomes dangerous for wild salmon too.
wichtigste: Despite its name, the salmon louse is not an insect but a small crustacean.
It lives as a parasite on salmon, sea trout and other salmonids in the sea.
It eats the mucus, skin and blood of its host.
Adult females grow to about one to two centimetres long.
In fish farms with many fish in a small space it multiplies strongly.
From fish farms, salmon lice can infest young wild salmon.
Against salmon lice, farmers use cleaner fish, among other things.

abschnitte.text: The salmon louse belongs to the **copepods**, a group of very small crustaceans. It has a flat body that clings like a sucker to the skin of the fish. The females carry long egg strings at the rear end. The salmon louse lives only in salt water and dies if the fish swims into fresh water.

abschnitte.titel: How does it harm the fish?
abschnitte.text: The salmon louse is a **parasite**, that is, an animal that lives at the expense of another. It rasps mucus, skin and blood off the fish. This creates wounds through which disease germs can enter. In a heavy infestation the fish is weakened and can even die.

In **fish farms** tens of thousands of salmon live in large net pens in the sea. For the salmon lice this is ideal, since they find very many hosts in a small space. Especially in Norway, Scotland, Ireland and Chile the salmon louse is a big problem for farming. Controlling it costs farmers a great deal of money every year.

Young wild salmon migrate from the rivers into the sea in spring. If their route passes fish farms, they can be infested by many salmon lice. Even a few lice can seriously harm a small young salmon. That is why experts blame lice from farms in part for wild salmon having become rare in some areas.

In the past mainly medicines were used against salmon lice, but the lice became increasingly resistant to them. Today many farms use **cleaner fish** such as wrasses or lumpfish, which eat the lice off the salmon. Other methods are warm water, freshwater baths or brushes. Some farms protect the fish with dense nets or raise them in closed tanks.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing that lives on or in another and harms it.
The animal on which a parasite lives.
A group of tiny crustaceans that occur in the sea and in fresh water.
A fish that frees other fish of parasites.

gewusst: Salmon lice attach themselves to the fish as tiny larvae and are hardly visible to the naked eye at first.
Fishers often recognise salmon freshly come up from the sea by the fact that salmon lice are still hanging on them.

teile.einleitung: A cat’s tongue feels rough like sandpaper. This is because of many small barbs with which the cat combs and cleans its fur. The cat’s tongue is an amazing tool for cleaning, drinking and eating.
wichtigste: The cat’s tongue is rough because it has many small barbs.
The barbs are called papillae and are made of horn, like our fingernails.
With its tongue the cat combs its fur and removes dirt and loose hairs.
The papillae take up saliva and carry it deep into the fur.
When drinking, the cat pulls up a small column of water with the tip of its tongue.
Cats cannot taste sweetness.
Cats sometimes bring swallowed hair back up as a hairball.

abschnitte.text: On a cat’s tongue sit hundreds of tiny barbs curved backwards. These **papillae** are made of keratin, that is, horn, like our fingernails. When a cat licks you, it therefore feels scratchy. In lions and tigers the papillae are so strong that they can scrape meat from bones.

Cats spend a large part of their waking time on **grooming**. The barbs work like the teeth of a comb and loosen tangles, dirt and loose hairs. In 2018 researchers discovered that the tips of the papillae are hollow and take up saliva. In this way the cat carries saliva deep into its fur, which cleans and cools.

Cats do not lap like dogs, which use their tongues like a scoop. The cat touches the surface of the water only briefly with the tip of its tongue and pulls the tongue back in a flash. This produces a small **column of water**, and the cat snaps up a mouthful from the top of it. It repeats this several times a second.

On the tongue there are also **taste buds**, but cats have far fewer of them than humans. Cats can taste well whether something is bitter, sour or salty. They cannot taste sweetness, however, because they lack the right sensory cells. As pure meat-eaters they do not need this taste either.

When grooming, the cat swallows many loose hairs. Most pass through the gut, but some collect in the stomach as a **hairball**. The cat then brings this back up. Regular brushing, especially in long-haired cats, helps against it.

Researchers in the USA studied the cat’s tongue closely and rebuilt it with a 3D printer. This gave rise to the idea for a special **hairbrush** that is easy to clean. The model could also be useful for animal care and for cleaning devices. When technology learns from nature, this is called **biomimetics**.
