begriffe.erklaerung: Small bumps on the tongue, shaped like barbs in cats.
The horn substance that hair, claws and fingernails are also made of.
A sense organ on the tongue with which you taste.
Technology that copies ideas from nature.

gewusst: The chocolate sweet called a cat’s tongue is named after the shape of the tongue, not its roughness.
A cat can also use its tongue to help cool down on hot days, because evaporating saliva cools.

teile.einleitung: The lion is a large big cat and is often called the ‘king of the beasts’. It lives mainly in the African savanna and is the only cat that lives together in groups, the prides. Its roar can be heard for kilometres.
wichtigste: The lion belongs to the cat family.
It lives mainly in the African savanna, with a small group in India too.
Lions live in prides of related females, their young and one or more males.
Males are larger and heavier than females and have a mane.
Over a short distance a lion runs at about 60 kilometres per hour.
Lions do not hunt successfully every day and then eat a lot at once.
Lions are considered threatened today.

abschnitte.text: After the tiger, the lion is the second largest cat in the world. Males usually weigh about 150 to 250 kilograms, females about 110 to 180 kilograms. The coat is sand-coloured, and at the end of the tail sits a dark tuft. Only the males wear a **mane**, by which you can recognise them from far away.

Lions today live mainly in the **savannas** and open woodlands of Africa south of the Sahara, for example in the Serengeti in Tanzania. They drink water from waterholes or rivers, but can also manage a few days without. A small group of Asiatic lions lives in the **Gir Forest** in India. In the past there were lions in North Africa, the Middle East and even in south-eastern Europe too.

A **pride** usually consists of several related females, their young and one or a few males. The males defend the territory and roar loudly to show others who the area belongs to. Young males must leave the pride at about two to three years old. Later they try to take over a pride themselves.

Usually the females hunt together and creep up on zebras, wildebeest, antelopes or buffalo. For a short sprint they reach about 60 kilometres per hour, but only over a short distance. When hunting they extend their sharp **claws**, otherwise they retract them so that they do not get blunt. Because not every hunt succeeds, lions do not eat every day, but eat a great deal at once.

Lions often rest and sleep for up to 20 hours a day to save energy. When they are not hunting, they walk leisurely and slowly. They are active mainly at dusk and at night, because they see much better in the dark than humans. After a gestation of about three and a half months the female usually gives birth to two to four **cubs**.

The number of lions has fallen sharply in recent decades, and they are considered **threatened**. Reasons are the loss of habitat, conflicts with livestock keepers and poaching. As a symbol of strength and courage the lion appears in many coats of arms and stories. In Switzerland the famous **Lion Monument** in Lucerne commemorates Swiss Guards who died in Paris in 1792.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large cat that hunts other animals, such as the lion, tiger or leopard.
A group of animals that live and hunt together.
Grassland with scattered trees in warm regions.
An area that an animal or a group defends against others.

gewusst: The roar of a lion can be heard up to about eight kilometres away.
In the pride, lionesses sometimes also suckle the young of other females.
The lion is the only cat species in which males and females look so different.

teile.einleitung: Rattlesnakes are venomous snakes from the Americas that warn with a rattle on the tail. When they feel threatened, they shake this rattle so fast that a loud buzzing sound is produced. With it they say: don’t come too close!
wichtigste: Rattlesnakes belong to the vipers and, among them, to the subfamily of pit vipers.
They form two genera: Crotalus and Sistrurus.
The name Crotalus comes from the Greek ‘krotalon’ and means castanet or rattle.
Carl Linnaeus described the genus Crotalus in 1758.
The rattle is made of keratin, and a new segment is added with every moult.
You cannot read the snake’s age from the age of the rattle.
Rattlesnakes live only in the Americas, from Canada to South America.

abschnitte.text: Rattlesnakes belong to the family of **vipers** and to the subfamily of pit vipers. There are two genera: the large genus Crotalus and the small genus **Sistrurus** with three species today. Sistrurus means ‘tail-rattler’, and these snakes are recognised by nine large scales on the head. The best-known species is the western diamondback, and the largest is the eastern diamondback in the south-east of the USA, which can grow to over 2 metres long.

The **rattle** is made of keratin, the same substance as our fingernails. It is built of hollow segments that fit loosely into each other and strike against one another when shaken. With every moult a new segment forms. Because the snake moults several times a year and segments can also break off, the rattle does not reveal its age.

abschnitte.titel: Seeing heat with the pit organ
abschnitte.text: Between the eye and the nostril, the rattlesnake has a small pit on each side. This **pit organ** senses heat radiation. In this way the snake can locate warm prey such as mice even in complete darkness. All pit vipers have this special sense organ.

Rattlesnakes live in North, Central and South America, with especially many species in Mexico and the south-west of the USA. They are found in deserts, prairies, forests and mountains. They eat mainly mice, rats, rabbits and sometimes birds or lizards. They kill their prey with a **venomous bite** and then swallow it whole.

Rattlesnakes do not lay eggs but give birth to live young. A newborn rattlesnake has only a ‘**prebutton**’ at the tip of the tail, which cannot rattle yet. Only after the first moults does a rattle form that makes noise. Even the young, however, have effective venom.

A bite can be dangerous for people, but with **antivenom** in hospital it is usually treated well. Rattlesnakes do not attack of their own accord, but warn first with their rattle. Anyone who hears the warning should walk slowly back. In Switzerland there are no rattlesnakes; only two native vipers live here: the asp viper and the adder.

begriffe.erklaerung: Vipers with a heat-sensing organ between the eye and the nose.
A firm horn substance that hair, nails and feathers are also made of.
The snake sheds its old skin, which has become too tight.
A medicine that cancels out the effect of snake venom.

gewusst: A rattlesnake can shake its rattle dozens of times a second without tiring quickly.
Even a freshly killed rattlesnake can still bite through reflexes, so you should never touch it.

teile.einleitung: The European garden spider is one of the best-known spiders in Europe and often lives right in our gardens. It gets its German name, Kreuzspinne or ‘cross spider’, from the pale patches on its back, which form a cross. It is famous for its skilful orb webs, which glisten in the morning dew in autumn.
wichtigste: The garden spider has four pairs of legs, so eight legs, and eight eyes.
Its body is about as big as a fingernail.
The female is usually clearly larger than the male.
It builds large orb webs to catch insects.
Its bite is harmless to people, at most like a small sting.
An adult garden spider usually lives about a year.
In winter most adults die, and only the eggs in the cocoon survive.

abschnitte.text: The **garden cross spider** is the commonest cross spider in Switzerland. Its round abdomen is brown to reddish and bears pale patches that form a cross. Like all spiders it has eight legs and eight eyes, but no wings and no antennae. The female is about as big as a fingernail, while the male stays much smaller.

The garden spider builds an **orb web** with spokes and a sticky catching spiral. A web can be over 30 centimetres across. Often it builds it anew every day and eats the old threads, to reuse the valuable silk. It does not stick fast itself, because it walks on non-sticky threads and has oily feet.

In its web the garden spider catches flies, midges, wasps and other insects. If an animal struggles in the web, it feels this through a signal thread. It paralyses the prey with a venomous bite and wraps it in silk. Then it injects digestive juice into it and sucks the prey dry.

In late summer and autumn the garden spiders are fully grown and mate. The male approaches carefully, because he is sometimes eaten by the female. Afterwards the female lays her eggs in a **cocoon** of spider silk and hides it. The adults die in winter, and in spring many tiny young spiders hatch.

Garden spiders are peaceful and mostly flee or sit still when a person comes. Their bite is at most like a small mosquito bite. They are useful for garden and house, because they catch many midges and flies. Their **spider silk** is very tear-resistant in relation to its weight and is closely studied by researchers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A round spider’s web with spokes like a bicycle wheel.
A protective covering of spider silk for the eggs.
The fine, very strong thread that spiders make from spinning glands.
An animal group with eight legs that includes spiders, scorpions and ticks.

gewusst: A garden spider often needs less than an hour for a whole orb web.
Spiders are not insects, because insects have only six legs.

teile.einleitung: The great tit is the largest and one of the commonest tits in Switzerland. You recognise it by its yellow belly with the black stripe and the black cap on its head. In winter it is a busy visitor to the bird feeder.
wichtigste: The great tit has a yellow belly and a black cap on its head.
In the male the black stripe on the belly is broader than in the female.
It lives in woods, parks and gardens and nests in tree hollows and nest boxes.
It eats mainly insects in summer and seeds in winter.
Because it eats many pests, it is popular with gardeners.
In great cold it fluffs up its plumage to stay warm.
A great tit can raise one or two broods a year.

abschnitte.text: The great tit is about 14 centimetres long and weighs around 16 to 21 grams, about as much as four sugar cubes. It has a glossy black **cap**, white cheeks and a yellow belly. A black **stripe** runs down the chest and belly. In the male it is broader and reaches down between the legs, in the female it is narrower.

Great tits live all over Europe, in parts of North Africa and far into Asia. In Switzerland they are among the commonest **breeding birds** and occur from the lowlands up to mountain forests. They are found in deciduous and mixed woods, parks, orchards and gardens in the middle of towns. Most stay here in winter too and are **resident birds**.

In spring and summer, great tits eat mainly insects, caterpillars and spiders. Larger insects they hack into pieces with the beak before eating them. In autumn and winter they eat seeds, nuts and berries. In doing so they hold a seed down with their **feet** and hack it open, and sometimes they hide seeds as a store for winter.

Great tits nest in **hollows**, for example in old woodpecker holes, cracks in walls or nest boxes. The female builds a soft nest of moss, hair and feathers and usually lays 6 to 12 eggs. While she incubates for about two weeks, the male brings her food. Both parents then feed the young with hundreds of caterpillars a day, and often a second brood follows.

In great cold the great tit fluffs up its **plumage**, so that a warming layer of air forms between the feathers. At night it often sleeps in a tree hollow or a nest box. At the bird feeder it first approaches cautiously and watches its surroundings. Then it usually takes a seed and flies off with it, to eat it in peace on a branch.

The song of the great tit sounds like ‘zi-zi-beh’ or ‘zizibe’ and can be heard from the end of January. Great tits also have many different **calls**, with which they warn of enemies, for example. They learn very easily and pick up tricks from other tits. That is why they are considered especially clever birds.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird that nests in an area and raises its young there.
A bird that stays in the same area all year round and does not migrate.
A small wooden box with an entrance hole in which hole-nesting birds can build their nest.
The eggs or young of a pair of birds from one nest.

gewusst: During the nestling period, a pair of great tits feeds thousands of caterpillars to its young.
In England, tits once learned to peck open the caps of milk bottles on the doorstep to get at the cream.

teile.einleitung: The saithe is a sea fish from the North Atlantic that is usually sold in shops in German-speaking countries under the name Seelachs (‘sea salmon’). Despite this name it is not a salmon, but a close relative of the cod. Its flesh is used, for example, to make fish fingers.
wichtigste: The saithe is a sea fish from the cod family.
In trade it is called Seelachs, but it is not a true salmon and belongs to the cod-like fish.
It lives in the North Atlantic, for example in the North Sea and around Norway and Iceland.
Its German name Köhler comes from its dark back, which is reminiscent of coal.
Saithe swim in large shoals and hunt smaller fish.
It usually grows to 60 to 100 centimetres long.
Its white flesh is often made into fillets and fish fingers.

abschnitte.text: The saithe has a slender, powerful body with three dorsal fins and two anal fins. Its back is dark greenish to almost black, the belly silvery pale. A pale **lateral line** along the body is clearly visible. It usually grows to 60 to 100 centimetres long, and large animals reach more than a metre.

Saithe live in the **North Atlantic**, from the North Sea via Norway and Iceland to the coast of North America. Young saithe often stay close to the coast. Older animals move into deeper water, usually down to about 200 metres, sometimes deeper. They form large **shoals** and travel long distances over the course of the year.

Young saithe eat small crustaceans. Adults are skilful **predators** and hunt herring, sprats and other smaller fish. In a shoal they sometimes drive their prey together. They themselves are eaten by larger fish, seals and seabirds.

The name **Seelachs** (‘sea salmon’) is a trade name that was meant to make the fish more popular. The saithe has nothing to do with true salmon; it belongs to the **cod-like fish** such as cod and haddock. In the past, smoked saithe flesh was dyed red and sold as a ‘salmon substitute’. The Alaska pollock, from which many fish fingers are made, is also a different kind of cod-like fish.

The saithe is an important **food fish** in Europe. It is caught mainly off Norway, Iceland and the Faroe Islands with trawl nets. Its lean, white flesh reaches the shops as fillets, frozen or in fish fingers. To stop the stocks being overfished, there are catch quotas, and some fisheries carry a sustainability label.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of sea fish that includes cod, haddock and saithe.
A sense organ along the body of a fish that senses water movements.
The name under which a product is sold in the shop.
A fixed amount of fish that may be caught in a year.

gewusst: The German name Köhler recalls the charcoal burners who used to make charcoal in the forest and were often blackened with soot.
Under the name Seelachs, shops sell two different fish species, the saithe and the Alaska pollock.

teile.einleitung: A cloven hoof (in German a Klaue) is the split hoof of animals such as the cow, goat, sheep, pig or chamois. Each foot carries two large horn shoes side by side, which together look like a divided hoof. Animals with such feet are called even-toed ungulates.
wichtigste: Cloven hooves are the horn shoes on the toes of even-toed ungulates.
A goat has two hooves on each foot, because it is an even-toed ungulate.
Hooves are made of hard horn, that is, keratin.
Underneath lie soft, elastic pads.
Because the hooves are movable, they adapt well to rock and give goats and chamois a grip.
Behind the main hooves, many animals have two small dewclaws.
In farm animals the hooves have to be cared for and trimmed regularly.

abschnitte.text: In even-toed ungulates the animals walk on the tips of two toes, the third and fourth toe. Each of these toes sits in a hard shoe of **horn**, the hoof. Together the two hooves form a split hoof. By contrast, the horse has only a single large toe with a whole hoof.

On the outside the hoof has a hard **horn wall** that keeps growing like a fingernail. Underneath lies the sole, and at the back is a soft, elastic **pad**. The pad absorbs shocks and, like a rubber sole, provides grip. A little further up the leg, cattle, goats and deer have small **dewclaws**, which usually do not touch the ground.

Goats, ibex and chamois are excellent climbers. Their two hooves can be spread a little and so adapt to rock edges and uneven ground. The hard rims grip like the edges of ski boots, and the rubbery pads stick to smooth stone. That is why chamois in the Swiss Alps can climb safely on steep rock faces.

In the barn the hooves often wear down less than on stony ground. That is why a **hoof trimmer** usually trims them in cows once or twice a year. Hooves that are too long or diseased hurt the animals and make them limp. Good hoof care is therefore important for the animals’ welfare.

Well known is **foot-and-mouth disease**, a very contagious viral disease of even-toed ungulates. It causes blisters in the mouth and on the hooves. In Switzerland it has not occurred for many decades, but it is strictly monitored. More common are inflammations between the hooves, caused by wet and dirty floors.

The German word Klaue is sometimes also used for the pointed **claws** of predators or birds of prey. People speak, for example, of the claws of an eagle or a bear. In zoology, however, Klaue mainly refers to the split hooves of even-toed ungulates. That is also where the German name Klauentiere (cloven-hoofed animals) for cattle, sheep, goats and pigs comes from.

begriffe.erklaerung: Animals that walk on two toes, each with a hoof, for example the cow and goat.
A small extra toe behind the main hooves that usually does not touch the ground.
The soft, springy part at the back of the hoof.
A professional who trims and cares for the hooves of farm animals.

gewusst: The horn wall of a cow’s hoof grows about half a centimetre a month.
Thanks to their hooves, chamois can dare leaps of several metres onto narrow rock ledges.

teile.einleitung: The Cuculiformes are an order of birds to which our well-known cuckoo belongs. Worldwide there are over 140 species, living mainly in warm countries. Not all of them lay their eggs in strange nests, and many raise their young themselves.
wichtigste: The cuckoo belongs to the bird group of the Cuculiformes.
Worldwide there are over 140 species of Cuculiformes.
Most species live in the tropics and subtropics.
Cuculiformes have feet with two toes pointing forwards and two backwards.
Only some of the species are brood parasites.
They also include the roadrunner from North America.
In Switzerland only one species breeds, the cuckoo.

abschnitte.text: The **Cuculiformes** form an order of their own in the bird world. They include cuckoos, coucals, anis and roadrunners. The birds differ greatly in size, from sparrow-sized to crow-sized species. Many have a long tail and a slightly curved beak.

Cuculiformes have so-called **zygodactyl feet**: two toes point forwards and two backwards. In this way they can sit and climb well on branches. Their plumage is often grey, brown or black, and some species shine green or blue. Many Cuculiformes eat insects, especially caterpillars.

Many people think all cuckoos are **brood parasites**. But only some of the species lay their eggs in strange nests, for example the cuckoo or the koel from Asia. Many other species build their own nests and feed their young themselves. The anis of South America even breed in groups in a shared nest.

The **roadrunner** lives in the deserts of North America and can run very fast. It hunts lizards, insects and even small snakes. As the cartoon character Road Runner it has become world famous. The coucals in Africa and Asia live in dense undergrowth and are reluctant to fly.

In central Europe and Switzerland only a single species breeds, the **cuckoo**. In the Mediterranean region the great spotted cuckoo also lives, which lays its eggs mainly in the nests of magpies. Rarely, a great spotted cuckoo also strays north of the Alps. Most species of the order, however, are found in Africa, Asia, Australia and America.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large group of related animal families in biology.
A bird’s foot with two toes pointing forwards and two backwards.
An animal that has others raise its young.
The hot regions of the Earth around the equator.

gewusst: The roadrunner would rather run than fly.
The turacos of Africa were once counted among the Cuculiformes, but today form a group of their own.

teile.einleitung: Salmon are powerful fish that live in the sea but return to spawn in the rivers where they hatched. On this journey they even leap over waterfalls. Their pink flesh is also a popular food in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Salmon travel from the sea upstream to spawn there.
They find their home river mainly with their sense of smell.
There is the Atlantic salmon and several species of Pacific salmon.
After spawning many salmon are badly weakened, and Pacific salmon all die.
Their dead bodies supply nutrients to animals and plants along the rivers.
In the past salmon swam up the Rhine as far as Switzerland.
A large part of the salmon in shops today comes from fish farms.

abschnitte.text: Salmon have a slim, powerful body with silvery, shiny scales. Like all **salmonids**, they have a small adipose fin on the back in front of the tail fin. An Atlantic salmon can grow to over a metre long. At spawning time many salmon turn red or brown, and in Pacific salmon often bright red.

abschnitte.titel: A life between river and sea
abschnitte.text: Salmon hatch in the gravel of a river and usually stay there for one to three years. Then they migrate to the sea, where they find plenty of food and grow quickly. After a few years they return to exactly the river where they were born. This migration is called **anadromous**, and they find the way mainly with their sense of smell.

On the way upstream the salmon eat nothing more and live off their fat reserves. They swim against strong currents and leap over rapids and small waterfalls. In North America **grizzly bears** often wait at such places and catch the leaping fish. At the destination the female lays her eggs in a spawning pit in the gravel.

After spawning many salmon are badly weakened. In Pacific salmon all the animals die, and only some Atlantic salmon can spawn several times. The dead fish are important for nature: their bodies supply **nutrients** for bears, birds, insects and even for the trees on the bank. In this way salmon carry nutrients from the sea deep inland.

Until the 19th century salmon swam up the Rhine as far as Basel and on into the Aare and Limmat. Because of power stations, pollution and overfishing, the salmon disappeared from Switzerland around the middle of the 20th century. Today the countries along the Rhine are trying to bring it back with **fish ladders** and clean water. Most salmon in Swiss shops come from fish farms, for example in Norway or Scotland.

begriffe.erklaerung: The name for fish that live in the sea and migrate into rivers to spawn.
The laying and fertilising of eggs in fish.
A staircase of pools with which fish can get past a power station or weir.
A small fin without rays between the dorsal fin and the tail fin.

gewusst: On their migration salmon can leap over obstacles about three metres high.
The pink colour of salmon flesh comes from pigments in the small crustaceans that the salmon eat.

teile.einleitung: The cowbell is a bell that cows wear on a leather strap around the neck. In Switzerland its sound belongs to the Alps as much as the mountains themselves. In the past it helped above all to find the animals again on wide pastures.
wichtigste: Many alpine cows in Switzerland wear a bell around the neck.
From the sound the herdsman knows where his animals are grazing.
A distinction is made between cast bells and forged Treicheln.
At the Alpaufzug and Alpabzug, cows wear especially large, decorated bells.
The straps are often skilfully embroidered or decorated.
In some villages there are arguments about the noise of cowbells.
Cowbells are also a popular souvenir and gift.

abschnitte.text: A cowbell is a sound instrument that hangs on a wide **bell strap** around a cow’s neck. Inside swings a clapper that strikes the wall with every movement. In this way you can hear the cow from far away. Goats and sheep also sometimes wear smaller bells.

In Switzerland a distinction is made between two kinds. A **bell** is cast from bronze or brass and sounds bright. A **Treichel** is forged from sheet iron and has a deeper, rough tone. Treicheln are often very large and heavy and are worn mainly on special occasions.

On the alp the cows graze in summer over large areas, often without a fence. In fog, in the forest or on steep ground you cannot always see them. From the sound of the bells the Senn, the alpine dairyman, knows where his herd is at the moment. Experienced herdsmen can even recognise individual animals by the tone of their bell.

At the **Alpaufzug**, the procession up to the alp in early summer, and at the Alpabzug in autumn, the cows wear especially large and beautifully decorated bells and Treicheln. The animals are also decorated with flowers and wreaths. At festivals, groups of Treichler also walk through the villages in traditional costume with large Treicheln. For the Silvesterchläuse in Appenzellerland, bells and rolls are an essential part of the custom.

Today some people ask whether heavy bells bother the cows. That is why many animals wear lighter bells in everyday use, and the large ones only on festive days. In some villages residents complain about the jingling at night, and municipalities then look for solutions. For many farmers, though, the bell is an important piece of tradition.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large cowbell forged from sheet metal with a deep sound.
The movable part inside the bell that produces the sound.
The festive journey of the cows up to the alp in early summer.
A herdsman on the alp who looks after the cows and often makes cheese.

gewusst: Large festival Treicheln can weigh several kilograms.
Cowbells are sometimes also used as a musical instrument in orchestras or at football matches.

teile.einleitung: The common woodlouse is a small, grey creepy-crawly that is often found under stones, in compost or in damp cellars. Although it lives on land, it is not an insect but a crustacean. It helps to turn dead plant material into fertile soil.
wichtigste: Common woodlice like to live in cellars and in damp, dark places.
They are crustaceans and related to crabs and lobsters.
Common woodlice have 14 legs, that is, seven pairs of legs.
They need moisture, because otherwise they dry out.
They eat mainly dead plant material.
The females carry their eggs in a brood pouch on the belly.
Common woodlice are harmless to people.

abschnitte.text: The **common woodlouse** belongs to the woodlice and so to the **crustaceans**. Its ancestors lived in the sea, but land woodlice have managed to live on land. Common woodlice grow to just under two centimetres long. Their body is flat and grey and covered with an armour of plates.

Common woodlice have seven pairs of legs, so 14 legs, and two pairs of antennae, one pair of which is tiny. Their armour is rough and grainy. At the back of the body sit two short projections. Unlike the related **pill woodlouse**, the common woodlouse cannot roll itself up into a ball.

Common woodlice need it damp and dark, because otherwise they dry out quickly. You find them under stones, boards, leaves and bark, in compost and in damp cellars. During the day they hide, at night they go looking for food. They live in Europe and have been carried to many other parts of the world.

Common woodlice eat mainly dead plant material such as leaves, rotting wood and fungi. They are **decomposers**, which means they help to turn plant remains into humus. In compost and in the garden they are therefore useful. They only rarely eat healthy plants.

Because woodlice descend from sea animals, they breathe with gill-like organs on their rear legs. Common woodlice also have fine breathing tubes there, called **pseudotracheae**, with which they breathe air. These only work, however, if they stay moist. That is why woodlice avoid dry, sunny places.

The female carries her eggs in a fluid-filled **brood pouch** on the underside of her body. In it the young develop and hatch as small, pale woodlice. Because the armour does not grow with them, woodlice have to moult. They moult in two steps, first the rear half of the body and later the front half.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of armoured animals that includes crabs, lobsters and woodlice.
Living things that break down dead plants and animals.
Shedding the old skin or armour in order to grow.
A pocket on the belly in which the eggs develop in safety.

gewusst: The common woodlouse is more closely related to a crab than to a beetle.
A half-moulted woodlouse looks two-coloured, grey at the front and pale at the back.

teile.einleitung: The Ensifera are grasshopper relatives with very long antennae, which are often longer than their whole body. They include the great green bush-cricket and the crickets. In summer you can hear their chirping in meadows and gardens, especially in the evening.
wichtigste: The great green bush-cricket belongs to the Ensifera.
You recognise Ensifera by their very long antennae.
They include bush-crickets and crickets.
They chirp by rubbing their forewings together.
Their ears sit on the front legs.
Many females have a sabre-shaped ovipositor.
Unlike grasshoppers, many Ensifera also eat insects.

abschnitte.text: The **Ensifera** are one of the two large groups of grasshopper relatives. The other group is the Caelifera, which includes the grasshoppers. Ensifera have thin antennae that are often longer than the whole body. They include bush-crickets such as the **great green bush-cricket**, but also crickets and the mole cricket.

The males chirp by rubbing their **forewings** together, with a kind of file on one wing and an edge on the other. Grasshoppers, by contrast, make their sounds with their hind legs. Each species has its own song, which is how males and females find each other. The ears of the Ensifera lie on the tibiae of the front legs and look like small slits.

Ensifera live in meadows, hedges, woods, gardens, and some also in caves or houses. Many are active mainly at dusk and at night. They eat plants, but often also insects such as caterpillars and aphids. The great green bush-cricket is a real hunter and can bite hard with its mouthparts.

The females of many species have a long, sabre-shaped **ovipositor** at the rear of the abdomen. With it they lay their eggs in the ground or in plant stems. In many species the eggs overwinter, and in spring small larvae hatch. These already look like the adults and moult several times until they get wings.

In Switzerland there are over 100 species of grasshopper and relatives, and a large part of them are Ensifera. Common are the great green bush-cricket, the **field cricket** and the upland green bush-cricket. In spring the field cricket sits in front of its burrow and chirps loudly. Because species-rich meadows are disappearing, some grasshopper species are threatened.

begriffe.erklaerung: Long sense organs on the head of insects for feeling and smelling.
A long extension on the abdomen of females for laying eggs.
Grasshopper relatives with short antennae, for example grasshoppers.
The juvenile form of an insect.

gewusst: In some crickets you can roughly estimate the air temperature from the number of chirps per minute.
The great green bush-cricket can be longer with wings and antennae than a child’s finger.

teile.einleitung: A sewage treatment plant cleans the dirty water from houses, schools and factories before it flows back into rivers and lakes. In Switzerland it is usually called an ARA, which stands for Abwasserreinigungsanlage (wastewater treatment plant). Thanks to sewage treatment plants, Swiss waters are clean again today, and fish and other water animals can live in them well.
wichtigste: A sewage treatment plant cleans wastewater so that rivers and lakes stay clean.
In Switzerland almost all households are connected to a sewage treatment plant.
The water is cleaned mechanically, biologically and chemically.
In biological cleaning, tiny bacteria eat the dirt.
The building of sewage treatment plants helped the Swiss lakes to recover.
Many plants are getting an additional stage against residues of medicines and chemicals.
Biogas can be obtained from sewage sludge.

abschnitte.text: **Wastewater** is all the water that we have used: from the toilet, shower, washing machine and kitchen. Added to this is water from factories and often also rainwater from roads and roofs. It flows through the sewer system, a network of underground pipes, to the sewage treatment plant. Without cleaning it would badly pollute streams and lakes.

First a **screen** holds back coarse things, for example wet wipes, plastic or leaves. In the grit chamber, sand and small stones sink to the bottom. In the primary settling tank the water flows very slowly, so that further particles of dirt can settle. After that the water is already clearer, but still contains many dissolved substances.

In the **aeration tank**, billions of tiny bacteria and other micro-organisms are at work. They eat the dissolved pollutants, in a similar way to what happens in nature. So that they have enough oxygen, air is blown into the tank. In the secondary settling tank the bacterial flocs settle as sludge, and the cleaned water flows on.

abschnitte.titel: Chemical cleaning and the fourth stage
abschnitte.text: With the help of chemicals, **phosphate** in particular is removed from the water. In a lake, phosphate acts like fertiliser and makes algae grow strongly. For some years now, Switzerland has been equipping many large sewage treatment plants with a fourth cleaning stage. It removes **micropollutants**, that is, tiny residues of medicines, plant protection products and cosmetics, for example with ozone or activated carbon.

In the 1960s and 1970s many Swiss lakes were badly polluted, and often you were not allowed to swim. Too much phosphate made algae run wild, and when the dead algae broke down, oxygen was lacking in the deep water. Fish such as whitefish suffered from this. Through the building of sewage treatment plants and a ban on phosphate in detergents in 1986, the lakes have recovered.

abschnitte.titel: What happens to the sewage sludge
abschnitte.text: A lot of **sewage sludge** is produced during cleaning. In large digester towers, bacteria break it down without oxygen, producing biogas. With it, the plant can generate electricity and heat. In Switzerland sewage sludge may no longer be spread on fields as fertiliser; it is burned instead.

begriffe.erklaerung: Short for Abwasserreinigungsanlage, which is what a sewage treatment plant is called in Switzerland.
An underground network of pipes that carries wastewater to the sewage treatment plant.
A tank in which bacteria clean the wastewater with the help of oxygen.
Sludge that settles during the cleaning of wastewater.
Tiny residues of medicines or chemicals in the water.

gewusst: Wet wipes do not belong in the toilet, because they do not dissolve and cause blockages in pumps and pipes.
The cleaned water from a sewage treatment plant is clean enough for fish, but still not drinking water.
The largest sewage treatment plant in Switzerland is the Werdhölzli plant in Zurich.

teile.einleitung: Lantern sharks are small sharks that live in the dark deep sea and can glow themselves. On their underside they carry tiny light organs that give off a faint blue light. In this way they are like living lanterns in the eternal darkness of the sea.
wichtigste: Lantern sharks form a family of their own among the sharks, with dozens of species.
They live in the deep sea, usually several hundred metres below the surface.
Many species hardly grow longer than half a metre.
On their belly sit thousands of small light organs.
The glow helps them to camouflage themselves from enemies below.
They include one of the smallest sharks in the world.
They give birth to live young.

abschnitte.text: Lantern sharks belong to the order of **dogfish sharks**, which have a spine in front of each dorsal fin. About 50 species are known worldwide. Most are smaller than half a metre, so much smaller than a great white shark. The dwarf lanternshark grows to only about 20 centimetres long and is among the smallest sharks of all.

Lantern sharks have thousands of tiny **light organs** in their skin, called photophores. In them a chemical reaction produces a faint blue light, which is called **bioluminescence**. The sharks can control the light with hormones and make it brighter or dimmer. In some species the spines on the dorsal fins also glow, perhaps as a warning to enemies.

Seen from below, an animal stands out as a dark outline against the faint remaining light from above. The glowing belly of the lantern shark evens out this shadow, so that it becomes almost invisible. This camouflage is called **counter-illumination**. Many deep-sea fish and squid also use this trick.

Lantern sharks live in all oceans, mainly on continental slopes and around undersea mountains. They usually stay at depths between about 200 and 1,500 metres, and some species even deeper. There it is cold, pitch dark and the water pressure is enormous. Some species rise a little higher at night to hunt.

Lantern sharks eat small fish, **squid** and crustaceans such as shrimps. Some species probably hunt in small groups. The females do not lay eggs in the water, but the young develop inside the mother and hatch from the egg case there. Afterwards they are born as fully formed small sharks.

Because lantern sharks live so deep, they are hard to observe. Many species were discovered only in recent decades, often because they ended up as **bycatch** in deep-sea nets. Researchers study their glow to learn more about camouflage and communication in the dark. The deep sea is still one of the least explored habitats on Earth.

begriffe.erklaerung: The ability of living things to make light themselves.
A small light organ in the skin of an animal.
Camouflage in which a glowing belly makes the animal’s own shadow disappear.
The part of the sea below about 200 metres, which hardly any sunlight reaches.
Animals that end up unintentionally in fishing nets.

gewusst: A fully grown dwarf lanternshark fits on a human hand.
The light of lantern sharks is blue because blue light travels furthest in water.
In the deep sea very many animals make their own light.

teile.einleitung: The kiwi is a flightless bird from New Zealand, about as big as a chicken. It is nocturnal, sniffs for worms with its long beak and has many features that you would otherwise expect more from mammals. For the people of New Zealand it is the most important national symbol.
wichtigste: The kiwi belongs to the flightless birds called ratites.
Its genus name Apteryx means ‘without wings’ and comes from George Shaw in 1813.
Today five living kiwi species are distinguished, all found only in New Zealand.
It is the only bird in the world with its nostrils at the tip of the beak.
Its feathers have no little hooks and therefore look like hair.
According to DNA studies, the extinct elephant bird of Madagascar is its closest relative.
Kiwis lay huge eggs in proportion to their body size.
Many kiwis are threatened by introduced predators.

abschnitte.text: A kiwi has a plump body, strong legs and a long, thin beak. Its wings are tiny and hidden under the brown plumage. The **feathers** have no little hooks joining their branches, and therefore feel like fur. The breastbone lacks the **keel** to which the flight muscles are attached in flying birds. The kiwi also has no preen gland, with which almost all birds oil their plumage.

The bones of most birds are hollow and filled with air so that they are light. The bones of the kiwi, by contrast, contain **bone marrow** as in mammals. Its body temperature is about 38 °C, which is lower than in most birds. The female also has two working ovaries, whereas in most birds only one works.

Kiwis live only in New Zealand, in forests, scrubland and grassland. Five species are distinguished, for example the **brown kiwi**, the little spotted kiwi and the Okarito kiwi. They belong to the flightless birds, like the ostrich, emu and rhea. DNA studies surprisingly showed that their closest relative is the extinct elephant bird of Madagascar.

Kiwis are nocturnal and see poorly. In return they have a very good **sense of smell**. Because their nostrils sit right at the tip of the beak, they can smell worms and insect larvae in the ground. They probe the earth with the beak and also eat spiders, fruit and seeds.

A kiwi egg is enormous compared with the bird and weighs up to a fifth as much as the female. In many species it is mainly the **male** that incubates the eggs. Incubation lasts about two and a half months, which is very long. The chicks hatch already covered in feathers and are soon independent.

In the past there were no mammals in New Zealand apart from bats. Introduced animals such as stoats, cats and dogs now kill many kiwis, above all chicks. That is why several species are **threatened**. New Zealand protects them with reserves, traps for predators and rearing stations for chicks.

begriffe.erklaerung: Large birds that cannot fly and get around by running, for example the ostrich, emu and kiwi.
An animal that is out and about at night and sleeps by day.
A gland at the base of the tail whose oil most birds use to care for their plumage.
A bony ridge on the breastbone of flying birds to which the powerful flight muscles attach.

gewusst: The people of New Zealand like to call themselves ‘Kiwis’.
The kiwi fruit was named after the bird, because its brown, hairy skin is reminiscent of its plumage.
Shortly before laying, a female kiwi carries an egg inside her that fills almost her whole belly.

teile.einleitung: The raven is the largest member of the crow family and at the same time the largest songbird in the world. It is completely black, very clever and can even use tools. After being rare in Switzerland for a long time, it can now be seen again in many regions.
wichtigste: The raven belongs to the crow family and to the genus Corvus, like the carrion crow and the rook.
It lives mainly in the Northern Hemisphere, in Europe, Asia and North America.
Ravens eat almost anything, for example carrion, small animals, eggs and fruit.
They are considered very intelligent and can use tools to get at food.
Pairs often stay together for life, and only the female incubates the eggs.
In human care a raven can live to over 40 years old.
Ravens traditionally live at the Tower of London, and a legend has grown up around them.

abschnitte.text: A raven is about 55 to 65 centimetres long and thus clearly larger than a carrion crow. Its wingspan can be well over a metre. Typical are the mighty beak, whose base is covered with **short, bristle-like feathers**, and the shaggy throat feathers. In flight you can recognise it by its **wedge-shaped tail** and its deep call ‘krock’.

The raven occurs in deserts, on sea coasts, in forests and in the high mountains. It lives in Europe, Asia, North America and parts of North Africa, even in the Arctic. In the Alps it often nests on rock faces. It needs large territories and mostly avoids densely built-up cities.

Ravens are **omnivores**. They eat carrion from dead animals, catch mice, insects and young birds and raid nests. Fruit, grain and rubbish are added to this. They often discover carcasses before other animals and sometimes lure foxes or wolves with them, which tear open the hide.

Ravens solve difficult tasks and use **tools**, for example little sticks to get food out of crevices. In experiments they even planned ahead and remembered who had treated them well or badly. They can imitate noises and sometimes human words. Young ravens like to play, for example by sliding in the snow or throwing objects through the air.

Raven pairs mostly stay together for life. In the **courtship season** they perform acrobatic flights with loops, rolls and dives. Early in the year, often in February or March, the female lays about 4 to 6 eggs in a large nest of branches. She incubates alone while the male brings food, and both then feed the young.

Because it ate carrion, in the Middle Ages the raven was often called the **gallows bird** and was thought to be a bringer of bad luck. In Norse legend the god Odin had two ravens called Hugin and Munin. Ravens are still kept at the Tower of London today, because according to legend the kingdom will fall if they leave the castle. In Switzerland the raven was rare for a long time because it was persecuted, and has only been spreading again for a few decades.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird family with ravens, crows, magpies and jays.
The flesh of dead animals.
An animal that eats both plants and animals.
Behaviour with which animals woo a partner.

gewusst: Ravens are songbirds, even though their croaking does not sound like singing at all.
Ravens can roll onto their backs in flight and glide upside down for a stretch.
Young ravens often join together in groups before they find a territory of their own.

teile.einleitung: A spawning pit is a small hollow in the gravel at the bottom of a river or stream into which fish lay their eggs. Trout and salmon in particular dig such pits. In them the eggs are well hidden and bathed by fresh water.
wichtigste: The pit in which a trout lays its eggs is called a spawning pit.
Trout lay their eggs in a pit of gravel on the river bed.
The female digs the pit with powerful strokes of her tail fin.
The male fertilises the eggs directly in the pit.
Afterwards the eggs are covered with gravel.
The eggs need clean gravel through which oxygen-rich water flows.
In Switzerland, brown trout usually dig their spawning pits between October and January.

abschnitte.text: A **spawning pit** is a shallow hollow in the gravel bed of a water that a female fish digs herself. Depending on the size of the fish, it is about the size of a plate up to the size of a bathtub. From above you can recognise it as a pale patch, because the gravel has been freshly turned over. Experts count such spots to find out how many fish are spawning in a stream.

The female lies on her side and beats powerfully against the bottom with her **tail fin**. In this way she stirs up sand and gravel, which are carried away by the current. This creates a hollow with clean, coarse gravel. The male guards the spot during this time and drives away rivals.

When the pit is ready, the female lays her eggs in it. At the same time the male releases his sperm fluid and **fertilises** the eggs. Afterwards the female digs a little further upstream and covers the eggs with gravel as she does so. In this way the eggs lie protected between the stones.

Between the stones fresh, oxygen-rich water flows through constantly. Depending on the water temperature, the eggs develop over several weeks to months. The hatched **yolk-sac larvae** stay at first in the gravel and live off their store of yolk. Only in spring do the young fish swim out of the gravel.

If a lot of fine silt gets into the stream, it clogs the gaps in the gravel. This is called **colmation**, and the eggs then suffocate because no more oxygen reaches them. Power stations that suddenly change the water level can also leave spawning pits dry. That is why in Switzerland new gravel is tipped in on some rivers, so that trout can find good spawning grounds again.

begriffe.erklaerung: The stony bottom of a river or stream.
A store of food on the belly of freshly hatched fish.
The clogging of the gaps in river gravel by fine silt.
The fusion of egg and sperm from which a new living thing arises.

gewusst: When laying her eggs, a female trout can make several spawning pits one after another.
Fishers and walkers should not walk through the gravel banks of trout streams in winter, because eggs may lie beneath them.

teile.einleitung: Hummingbirds are tiny, often iridescently coloured birds that occur only in the Americas. They can hover in the air like a helicopter and are the only birds that can even truly fly backwards. With their long beaks they drink nectar from flowers.
wichtigste: Hummingbirds form a bird family of their own with over 300 species.
They live only in North, Central and South America.
The smallest bird in the world is the bee hummingbird, a hummingbird from Cuba.
Hummingbirds can hover in the air and even fly backwards.
They often beat their wings more than 50 times a second.
Their most important food is sugary flower nectar, plus small insects.
In Switzerland there are no hummingbirds in the wild.

abschnitte.text: Most hummingbirds are only 6 to 12 centimetres long and weigh a few grams. The **bee hummingbird** measures about 5 to 6 centimetres and weighs around 2 grams, less than a sugar cube. The largest is the giant hummingbird from the Andes, at a good 20 centimetres. Many males have feathers that **shimmer** metallic green, red or violet depending on how the light falls.

Hummingbirds live only in the Americas, from Alaska to Tierra del Fuego. Most species are found in the tropical rainforests and mountain forests of South America, for example in Ecuador and Colombia. Some species live high in the Andes at over 4,000 metres. The **ruby-throated hummingbird** flies from North America to Central America in autumn and even crosses the Gulf of Mexico on the way.

Hummingbirds drink mainly **nectar**, a sugary liquid from flowers. To do so they put their beak deep into the flower and lick very fast with their long, forked tongue. For protein they also catch small insects and spiders. Because they use so much energy, they visit hundreds of flowers every day.

In hovering flight, hummingbirds rotate their wings at the shoulder and beat them back and forth in a lying figure of eight. In this way they can hover in front of a flower and fly sideways and backwards. Small species manage 50 to 80 **wingbeats** a second, which produces the typical hum. Their heart can beat over 1,000 times a minute in flight.

Hummingbirds are mostly loners and bravely defend their flowers against their own kind. The female builds a tiny nest alone from plant down and spider webs, which stretches as the chicks grow. In it she usually lays two white eggs that are hardly bigger than peas or beans. On cold nights hummingbirds fall into a stupor called **torpor** to save energy.

When they drink, pollen sticks to the head and beak. In this way hummingbirds **pollinate** many plants, which often have red, tube-shaped flowers. Some flowers and hummingbirds fit together as well as a key and a lock. Some species are threatened by the destruction of forests.

begriffe.erklaerung: Sweet juice in flowers that attracts animals.
Flight on the spot with very fast wingbeats.
A stupor in which body temperature and heartbeat drop sharply to save energy.
The transfer of pollen so that a plant can form seeds.

gewusst: What some people in Switzerland take for a hummingbird is usually the hummingbird hawk-moth, a moth that likewise hovers in front of flowers.
In proportion to its body size, a hummingbird has one of the largest hearts of all birds.
A hummingbird can drink more nectar in a day than it weighs itself.

teile.einleitung: Konrad Lorenz was an Austrian zoologist and is regarded as one of the founders of behavioural research. He became famous because young greylag geese followed him as if he were their mother. For his research he received the Nobel Prize in 1973.
wichtigste: Konrad Lorenz lived from 1903 to 1989 and came from Vienna.
He is regarded as one of the founders of comparative behavioural research, ethology.
He researched imprinting, in which young animals accept the first moving creature as their mother.
Gosling chicks that saw him after hatching followed him like their mother.
In 1973, together with Karl von Frisch and Nikolaas Tinbergen, he received the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine.
His books about animals became very well known.
His attitude during the time of National Socialism is viewed critically today.

abschnitte.text: Konrad Lorenz was born in Vienna in 1903 and grew up in Altenberg near Vienna. Even as a child he kept many animals, including ducks, geese and jackdaws. He first studied medicine and then **zoology**. Later he headed, among other things, a Max Planck Institute for Behavioural Physiology in Seewiesen in Bavaria.

Lorenz observed that freshly hatched gosling chicks follow the first moving creature they see. When he himself was there, the chicks ran after him as if he were their mother. He called this quick, lasting learning in a short span of time **imprinting**. The greylag goose Martina, who regarded him as her mother, became especially well known.

Lorenz wanted to understand why animals behave as they do. He observed animals as far as possible in their natural surroundings and compared the behaviour of different species. In this way he researched inborn behaviours, which he called **instinctive actions**. This made him a founder of **ethology**, the science of animal behaviour.

In 1973 Lorenz received the **Nobel Prize** in Physiology or Medicine together with the bee researcher Karl von Frisch and the Dutchman Nikolaas Tinbergen. He also became known through books for a wide public, such as ‘King Solomon’s Ring’ from 1949. In ‘On Aggression’ from 1963 he wrote about aggression in animals and humans. Later he also campaigned for environmental protection.

Konrad Lorenz joined the Nazi party in 1938 and in that period wrote texts that fitted the racial doctrine of the National Socialists. After the war he distanced himself from this, but many find his explanations inadequate. Some honours were therefore later taken away from him. That is why he is seen today as an important researcher, but also as a **controversial** person.

Imprinting is now an established term in biology and psychology. Findings from it help, for example, in raising young animals in zoos and rescue centres. In some reintroduction projects, chicks are raised in such a way that they do not imprint on humans. Konrad Lorenz died in 1989 at the age of 85.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science that researches the behaviour of animals.
Quick learning in a short phase of life that can hardly be undone.
Inborn behaviour that an animal does not have to learn.
A famous prize for outstanding achievements in science, literature and peace.

gewusst: In his parents’ house in Altenberg, Lorenz kept a colony of jackdaws whose birds flew freely in and out.
Lorenz researched not only geese but also jackdaws, fish and dogs.
The 1973 Nobel Prize was one of the first to be awarded for research into animal behaviour.

teile.einleitung: The kype is a hook-shaped outgrowth on the lower jaw of male salmon and trout. It forms mainly at spawning time. With it the males look especially fierce and show others how strong they are.
wichtigste: The kype grows on the lower jaw of male salmonids.
Male lake trout often develop it especially clearly at spawning time.
It is a sign of a fully grown male ready to spawn.
In fights over females it can serve as a weapon.
Often the male can no longer quite close his mouth because of the hook.
Together with the hook, the males get a coloured spawning dress.

abschnitte.text: The **kype** is an upward-curved extension of the lower jaw. It occurs in males of salmon, lake trout, sea trout and other salmonids. The hook arises because bone and tissue on the jaw grow strongly before the spawning season. Females usually have no hook or only a small one.

The hook grows when the males become sexually mature and move into the rivers at spawning time. In lake trout this is in autumn, when they ascend from the lakes into the inflowing streams. At the same time the fish change strongly in other ways too and get a coloured **spawning dress**. In Atlantic salmon that survive, the hook partly shrinks back again afterwards.

At spawning time the males fight for the best places near the females. They threaten, bite and ram each other. The kype makes the males larger and better able to defend themselves. For the females, a large hook is also a sign of a strong **male**.

Besides the hook, many salmonids change their appearance at spawning time. Lake trout become darker, salmon get reddish patches, and some Pacific salmon glow bright red. In the **pink salmon** the males even grow a high hump on the back. These changes cost a lot of energy, because the fish hardly eat during the spawning migration.

The **lake trout** lives in large Swiss lakes such as Lake Constance, Lake Geneva or Lake Lucerne. In autumn it migrates into the rivers and streams to spawn. Large males with a mighty kype are then an impressive sight. Because weirs and power stations block its way, the lake trout is threatened in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: The time of year in which fish reproduce.
The special colours that fish get at spawning time.
Grown up enough to be able to reproduce.
A large trout that lives in lakes and migrates into rivers to spawn.

gewusst: In some large male salmon the kype is so long that it fits into a pit in the upper jaw.
Fishers can easily tell from the kype whether they have caught a male or a female.

teile.einleitung: Heat, or being in season, is the time when a bitch is ready to mate and can have young. It normally comes about twice a year and lasts roughly three weeks. In other animals this time is called oestrus, in cats for example being on heat.
wichtigste: Heat is the fertile time of the bitch.
It normally occurs about twice a year.
A heat usually lasts around three weeks.
The first heat usually comes at the age of about six to twelve months.
Typical are a swollen vulva and bloody discharge.
Male dogs can smell a bitch in heat from far away.
Neutering ends the heats.

abschnitte.text: In dogs, heat is the time in which the female, the **bitch**, produces eggs and can become pregnant. It is controlled by **hormones**, that is, messenger substances in the body. In this time not only the body changes, but often also the behaviour. Many bitches are more clingy, more restless or mark more often with urine.

Most bitches come into heat about twice a year, so roughly every six months. Small breeds are often in heat for the first time at six months, large breeds sometimes only after a year. The interval between two heats is a little different for every bitch. There is no menopause as in humans in dogs, the intervals only get longer with age.

The heat has several stages. First comes **proestrus** of about nine days with bloody discharge, in which the bitch still turns male dogs away. Then follows **standing heat**, in which she lets herself be mated, usually also for about a week. Afterwards the body calms down again until the next heat.

A bitch in heat gives off scents that male dogs can smell over long distances. Some males then become very excited, howl, eat less or try to slip away. If the bitch is mated, she is **pregnant** for about nine weeks, so around 63 days. Afterwards usually several puppies are born.

During heat you should keep the bitch on the lead and away from strange male dogs. Against bloodstains in the home there are special protective pants. Anyone who does not want puppies can have the bitch **neutered** by the vet. In Switzerland you should discuss this well with the vet, because neutering has advantages and disadvantages.

Other mammals also have fertile periods, which are generally called **oestrus**. In cats it is called being on heat, in mares being in season and in deer the rut. In deer you can hear the loud roaring of the males in autumn. Each species has its own rhythm for this.

begriffe.erklaerung: A female dog.
A male dog.
Messenger substances that control processes in the body.
The word for an animal that carries young in its belly.
An operation after which an animal can no longer have young.

gewusst: Female wolves are in heat only once a year, domestic bitches usually twice.
The Basenji is a dog breed whose bitches often come into heat only once a year.
Some bitches have a false pregnancy after the heat and mother toys like puppies.

teile.einleitung: The red panda is a reddish-brown, climbing animal from the mountain forests of the Himalayas and south-west China. With its thick fur, white face and long, ringed tail, it looks almost like a soft toy. Although it is called a panda, it is not closely related to the giant panda.
wichtigste: The red panda is slightly larger than a house cat.
Its fur is mainly reddish-brown, the tail long and ringed.
It lives in the Himalayas and in south-west China.
It belongs to an animal family of its own, not to the family of the giant panda.
It is active mainly at dusk and at night.
Its main food is bamboo.
The red panda is endangered.

abschnitte.text: The red panda grows to about 50 to 65 centimetres in head and body length, plus a bushy tail of 30 to 50 centimetres. It usually weighs 3 to 6 kilograms. Its fur is **reddish-brown** on top, the belly and legs are dark, and the face has white markings. The tail is patterned with light and dark rings.

Red pandas live in cool mountain forests with dense bamboo undergrowth, often between 2,000 and 4,000 metres above sea level. They occur in Nepal, Bhutan, India, Myanmar and in south-west China. They spend most of their lives in the **trees**. In the cold they curl up and cover themselves with their tails like a blanket.

The red panda eats mainly the tender leaves and shoots of **bamboo**. Now and then it also eats fruit, berries, mushrooms, eggs or insects. Because bamboo provides little energy, it sleeps a lot and moves rather slowly. Like the giant panda, it has an enlarged wrist bone, a kind of **false thumb**, with which it can hold bamboo stalks.

Red pandas are active mainly at **dusk** and at night. During the day they usually rest on branches high up in the trees. They live as loners and mark their territory with scents. In summer, after a pregnancy of four to five months, usually one or two young are born.

The red panda was already described in 1825, long before Europeans knew the giant panda. It was therefore the first ‘panda’. For a long time researchers argued about whether it belongs to the bears or the raccoons. Today it stands in a family of its own, the **red panda family** (Ailuridae), and is only distantly related to the giant panda.

The red panda is classed as **endangered**. Its forests are being cut down, and sometimes the animals are poached or caught as pets. In the wild there are probably fewer than 10,000 adult animals. Zoos all over the world, including in Switzerland, take part in breeding programmes to preserve the species.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal family of its own, which today includes only the red panda.
An elongated bone at the wrist that helps like a sixth finger when gripping.
An animal that is out and about mainly in the evening and early morning.
An animal that mostly lives alone and not in a group.

gewusst: The English name ‘red panda’ simply means a panda that is red, and in China the animal is also called the ‘fire fox’.
The red panda can climb down tree trunks head first, because it can turn its hind feet backwards.

teile.einleitung: Cormorants are a family of dark, fish-eating water birds found all over the world. They are excellent divers and in Switzerland also eat popular food fish such as whitefish and grayling. That is why nature lovers admire them and fishers often view them critically.
wichtigste: The family of cormorants, or shags, includes about 40 species.
They occur on coasts and waters on every continent except Antarctica.
All cormorants are good divers and eat mainly fish.
In Switzerland the cormorant, Phalacrocorax carbo, is the commonest species.
The cormorant also eats whitefish, an important food fish of the Swiss lakes.
The Galápagos cormorant is the only species that cannot fly.
Many cormorants spread their wings to dry after diving.

abschnitte.text: Cormorants, also called **shags**, form the family Phalacrocoracidae with about 40 species. Most are black or black and white, and some have brightly coloured facial skin. Typical are a long neck, a hooked beak and feet on which all four toes are joined by webbing. The smallest species weigh under a kilogram, the largest over three kilograms.

Cormorants live on sea coasts, lakes and rivers almost everywhere in the world. Many species, such as the **shag**, live only by the sea, others inland as well. In Europe, besides the cormorant, the shag and the pygmy cormorant occur. There are especially many species in New Zealand and on the coasts of the Southern Hemisphere.

Cormorants hunt under water and drive themselves along with their feet as they do so. Sometimes they hunt in groups and herd **shoals of fish** together. They eat mainly fish that they can catch easily, that is, common species. Their plumage gets wet when diving, so afterwards they dry their wings in the sun.

On the Galápagos Islands lives the **Galápagos cormorant**. It has only small stub wings left and can no longer fly. Because there were no predators on the islands for a long time, it did not have to flee and found enough food in the sea. It is one of the rarest seabirds in the world.

In Switzerland cormorants also eat **whitefish**, perch and the threatened grayling. Professional fishers complain that the birds reduce their catches and damage fish in nets. Nature conservationists point out that over-fertilisation, climate change and river engineering also change fish stocks. The Confederation and the cantons try to take both interests into account with rules on regulation.

In China and Japan there has been **cormorant fishing** for over a thousand years. In it, trained birds catch fish for their keepers. In Japan it is still demonstrated as a tradition on the Nagara River today. On the coast of Peru, cormorants and other seabirds once supplied the valuable fertiliser guano with their droppings.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another name for cormorants.
A salmon-like fish from Swiss lakes that is popular to eat.
Fertiliser from the dried droppings of seabirds.
A large group of fish swimming together.

gewusst: The Galápagos cormorant is the only cormorant in the world that has lost the ability to fly.
Cormorant chicks put their whole head into their parents’ throat to be fed.
In winter there are clearly more cormorants in Switzerland than in summer, because birds from the north spend the winter here.

teile.einleitung: The Kodiak bear is an especially large subspecies of the brown bear. It lives only on Kodiak Island and the surrounding islands in the south of Alaska. Together with the polar bear, it is one of the largest predators that live on land.
wichtigste: The Kodiak bear is a subspecies of the brown bear.
It lives on Kodiak Island and neighbouring islands in Alaska.
Together with the polar bear, it is one of the largest land predators in the world.
Large males can weigh over 600 kilograms.
Standing upright, a large Kodiak bear is around 3 metres tall.
It eats salmon, berries, grass and roots.
In winter it spends the cold months in winter dormancy in a den.

abschnitte.text: The Kodiak bear is one of the largest **subspecies** of the brown bear. Males usually weigh 300 to over 600 kilograms, females are much lighter. When a large male stands on its hind legs, it is around 3 metres tall. That makes it much bigger than the brown bears in Europe, such as those that occasionally migrate into Switzerland from Italy.

Kodiak bears live only in the **Kodiak Archipelago**, a group of islands in the Gulf of Alaska. The landscape consists of mountains, meadows, forests and many rivers. Since the end of the last ice age about 12,000 years ago, the bears there have been separated from other brown bears. That is why they have developed into a subspecies of their own.

Kodiak bears are **omnivores**. In spring they eat grass and roots, in summer mainly salmon, which swim up the rivers to spawn. In late summer and autumn many berries are added. In this way they build up a thick layer of fat for the winter.

In winter the bears withdraw to a den and go into **winter dormancy**. They eat and drink nothing for months and live off their fat reserves. In the den the female usually gives birth to two or three very small cubs. The cubs stay with their mother for about three years.

Today about 3,500 Kodiak bears live on Kodiak Island. A large part of their habitat belongs to a **nature reserve**, the Kodiak National Wildlife Refuge. Hunting is strictly regulated, and the population is considered stable. For tourists there are guided trips on which you can watch the bears fishing from a safe distance.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of animals of one species that has developed slightly differently in a particular area.
A group of islands that lie close together.
An animal that eats both plants and meat.
A long resting state in winter from which the animal can wake up easily, however.

gewusst: A newborn Kodiak bear weighs less than half a kilogram, even though it later becomes so huge.
Kodiak bears sometimes stand on their hind legs, not to attack but to be able to smell and see better.

teile.einleitung: The cuckoo is a bird that almost every child recognises by its call ‘cuck-oo’. It is famous for laying its eggs in the nests of other birds. These foster parents then raise the strange, much larger chick.
wichtigste: The cuckoo is about as big as a pigeon, but slimmer.
It is a migratory bird and spends the winter in Africa south of the Sahara.
The female lays her eggs in the nests of other bird species.
Worldwide the cuckoo uses over 100 different species as host birds.
The cuckoo chick pushes the other eggs out of the nest with its back.
It likes best to eat caterpillars, including poisonous and hairy ones.
In Switzerland, for example, the reed warbler often raises young cuckoos.

abschnitte.text: The cuckoo is about as big as a pigeon, but slimmer, and has a long tail. Its back is grey, its belly pale with dark cross stripes. In flight it looks like a **bird of prey**, a bit like a sparrowhawk, which is why small birds are sometimes afraid of it. Only the male calls the familiar ‘cuck-oo’, while the female has a trilling call.

The cuckoo lives at woodland edges, in bogs, in reed beds and in open landscapes with bushes. It is a **migratory bird** and spends the winter in Africa south of the Sahara. In April it returns to Europe. The young cuckoos later fly to Africa entirely alone, without anyone showing them the way.

The female cuckoo does not build a nest of her own. She lays one egg at a time in the nest of another bird, often when that bird is not there. This way of reproducing is called **brood parasitism**. The cuckoo egg often looks very similar to the eggs of the host birds, so that it does not stand out.

The chick hatches after about two weeks, often earlier than the other young. After a short time it pushes the other eggs or chicks out of the nest with its back. It grows much faster and becomes much larger than its foster parents. They feed it all the same, because it begs especially loudly and insistently and shows a large, bright red gape.

The cuckoo eats mainly caterpillars, including poisonous and heavily hairy ones that other birds spurn. In this way it eats many **pest caterpillars** in the forest. In Switzerland, reed warblers, pied wagtails and black redstarts are common host birds. Because there are fewer insects and suitable habitats, the cuckoo has become rarer in many areas.

begriffe.erklaerung: When an animal has others incubate its eggs and raise its young.
A bird that incubates and feeds the cuckoo chick.
A bird that flies to warmer regions in autumn and returns in spring.
A caterpillar that eats many leaves and so harms trees.

gewusst: How a proper cuckoo calls is inborn in the young cuckoo, even though it grows up among strange birds.
If several female cuckoos lay in the same nest, usually only one of the cuckoo chicks survives.
An old proverb says that if you have money in your pocket at the first cuckoo call in spring, you will have enough all year.

teile.einleitung: Toads are amphibians that are closely related to frogs. They usually have dry, warty skin and move by crawling rather than hopping. In spring many toads migrate to their spawning waters and often need people’s help on the way.
wichtigste: Toads are amphibians, living on land and in water.
They have drier, warty skin than frogs.
Behind the eyes sit glands that release a venom against enemies.
The commonest toad in Switzerland is the common toad.
Toads lay their spawn in long strings.
In spring they often migrate back to the water in which they themselves hatched.
On many roads, toad fences and volunteer helpers assist with crossing.

abschnitte.text: Toads have a plump body, short legs and dry, **warty skin**. Frogs, by contrast, usually have smooth, moist skin and long jumping legs. Behind the eyes toads carry two large **parotoid glands**, from which they release a bitter venom when in danger. The females of the common toad are clearly larger than the males and can grow to over ten centimetres long.

Toads live in woods, gardens, meadows and fields. By day they hide under stones, leaves or in holes in the ground. At dusk and at night they go looking for food. They spend the winter in torpor in frost-free hiding places in the soil.

Toads eat snails, worms, beetles, spiders and other small animals. They snap up their prey with their sticky tongue, which they shoot out in a flash. That is why they are very useful helpers in the garden. As tadpoles, by contrast, they eat algae and plant remains.

In March and April common toads often migrate to the pond where they were born. The smaller males often let the female carry them piggyback on the way. In the water the female lays her **spawn** in long strings with thousands of eggs. Because many animals have to cross roads on the way, conservation groups put up **toad fences** and carry the animals safely across in buckets.

In Switzerland there are several species of toad, for example the common toad, the natterjack toad and the midwife toad. The midwife toad is also called the **Glögglifrosch** (‘little bell frog’) because of its bell-like call. In it, the male carries the strings of eggs around wound around his hind legs. Many species are threatened because ponds, pools and damp meadows have disappeared.

begriffe.erklaerung: Animals that are usually born in water and later also live on land, for example frogs and toads.
The eggs of amphibians or fish that are laid in water.
The larva of a toad or frog that lives in water.
A poison gland behind the eyes of toads.

gewusst: Common toads can live to several decades old in captivity.
In Australia the cane toad was introduced and is now a great pest there.

teile.einleitung: Lola ya Bonobo is a sanctuary for orphaned bonobos near Kinshasa, the capital of the Democratic Republic of the Congo. The name means ‘paradise of the bonobos’ in the Lingala language. Here young great apes whose mothers were killed by poachers are cared for.
wichtigste: Lola ya Bonobo is a rescue centre for orphaned bonobos.
It lies on the edge of Kinshasa in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.
The name means ‘paradise of the bonobos’ in Lingala.
It was founded by the conservationist Claudine André.
Female carers look after the bonobo babies like substitute mothers.
Some bonobos were later released back into the wild.
In the wild, bonobos live only in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

abschnitte.text: Lola ya Bonobo is a **rescue centre**, that is, a safe home for bonobos that have lost their mothers. It lies in wooded grounds with streams and small waterfalls on the edge of **Kinshasa**. The animals live there in large forest enclosures in groups. It is considered the only sanctuary of its kind specially for bonobos in the world.

The Belgian-Congolese conservationist **Claudine André** began in the 1990s to take in orphaned bonobos. From this came the sanctuary, which has been in its present place since 2002. It is run by the organisation ‘Les Amis des Bonobos du Congo’. By now many dozens of bonobos have found a home there.

Most bonobo babies come to Lola ya Bonobo because their mothers were hunted for **bushmeat**. The little ones are then often sold as pets and are ill, frightened and undernourished. In the centre, carers called ‘mamans’ look after them day and night. Later the young bonobos are gradually introduced to a group of their own kind.

A major aim is to let bonobos live in freedom again. From 2009 bonobos from Lola ya Bonobo were **released** for the first time in a protected forest area in the province of Équateur. This area is called Ekolo ya Bonobo, ‘land of the bonobos’. Researchers and rangers watch there how the animals cope.

Bonobos are **great apes** and, like chimpanzees, are among our closest relatives. They live only in the rainforests south of the Congo River. They are known for often settling quarrels peacefully and for living in groups in which females have a lot of influence. The species is **endangered**, above all because of poaching and the destruction of the forests.

Lola ya Bonobo receives many school classes and visitors from Kinshasa every year. They are to learn that bonobos are protected and must not be hunted or kept. In addition, researchers from all over the world study here how bonobos think, share and cooperate. In this way the centre helps the animals in several ways.

begriffe.erklaerung: A place where injured or orphaned wild animals are cared for.
Meat from hunted wild animals, often traded illegally.
Letting an animal go back into the wild.
A group of apes with gorilla, chimpanzee, bonobo and orang-utan.
An important language in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

gewusst: The genetic material of bonobos and humans is almost 99 per cent the same.
In experiments bonobos often voluntarily share food with strange members of their species.
Bonobos were described as a species of their own only in the 20th century, before that they were thought to be chimpanzees.

teile.einleitung: Cats have a typical predator’s set of teeth with pointed canines and sharp carnassial teeth. An adult cat normally has 30 teeth. Their teeth are made for gripping and cutting meat, not for thorough chewing.
wichtigste: An adult cat normally has 30 teeth.
Kittens first have 26 milk teeth.
The change of teeth is finished at about half a year old.
The long canine teeth are called fangs.
With the carnassial teeth the cat cuts meat like scissors.
Cats hardly chew their food; they swallow pieces whole.
Tooth problems are common in older cats.
