abschnitte.text: An adult cat normally has 30 teeth, which is fewer than the 32 of a human. In the upper jaw there are 16 teeth, in the lower jaw 14. There are small **incisors**, four long canines, and premolars and molars. All the teeth are pointed; a cat has no flat grinding teeth like humans.

The four long canine teeth are called **fangs** in predators. With them the cat grips its prey and kills it with a precise bite to the neck. Nerves in the teeth sense exactly where the bite has to land. The fangs are the most striking teeth in a cat’s mouth.

At the back of the jaw lie the **carnassial teeth**, one especially large tooth above and below on each side. They slide past each other like the blades of a pair of scissors and cut meat into pieces. That is why cats hardly chew, but swallow the chunks whole. That is why cats often tilt their heads when eating.

abschnitte.titel: Milk teeth and change of teeth
abschnitte.text: Kittens are born without teeth. After about two to three weeks the first **milk teeth** grow, 26 in all. From about three to four months they fall out and the permanent teeth grow in. At about half a year old the young cat has its full set of teeth.

Cats too can get **tartar**, gum inflammation and painful tooth damage. Because cats hide pain well, you often notice it only late. Signs are bad breath, drooling or poor eating. That is why the vet should also look at the teeth at the yearly check-up.

All cats, from the lion to the house cat, have a similar set of teeth. The longest fangs belonged to the extinct **sabre-toothed cats** such as Smilodon. Their upper canines were over 20 centimetres long. They died out at the end of the last ice age, about 10,000 years ago.

begriffe.erklaerung: A long, pointed canine tooth in predators for gripping prey.
A large, sharp cheek tooth that cuts meat like scissors.
The first teeth of a young mammal, which fall out later.
A hard deposit on the teeth.

gewusst: Cats have fewer teeth than dogs, which have 42.
Cats can hardly grind with their teeth; their jaw moves almost only up and down.

teile.einleitung: KORA is a Swiss organisation that researches and monitors large predators such as lynx, wolf and bear. It collects data so that the authorities and the public know how many of these animals live where. The name stands for ‘carnivore ecology and wildlife management’.
wichtigste: KORA stands for carnivore ecology and wildlife management.
The organisation is based in Ittigen near Bern.
In Switzerland it researches and monitors wolves, lynx, bears, golden jackals and wildcats, among others.
KORA grew out of a lynx project of the 1980s and has been a foundation since 2017.
It works closely with the Federal Office for the Environment (FOEN) and the cantons.
Important tools are camera traps and genetic samples.
KORA also informs the public about large predators.

abschnitte.text: KORA is a non-profit **foundation** based in Ittigen in the canton of Bern. It employs biologists who specialise in predators. It grew out of a research project on the lynx in the 1980s. Since 2017 KORA has been a foundation whose board includes representatives of public institutions.

The most important task is **monitoring**, that is, the regular surveillance of predator populations. KORA also researches how the return of wolf and lynx affects wild animals, farm animals and people. It advises the authorities, for example on implementing the hunting law. It also takes part in national and international working groups.

Lynx are often counted with **camera traps**, which trigger automatically when an animal walks past. Because every lynx has its own pattern of spots, individual animals can be recognised. For wolves, droppings, hairs or saliva on killed prey are collected for **genetic analyses**. Some animals also wear a collar with a transmitter that records their path.

The lynx was reintroduced in Switzerland from 1971, after it had been exterminated. The **wolf** returned by itself from Italy and appeared again in the Valais from 1995. Since then the wolf population has grown strongly and there are many packs. Individual bears also keep migrating from Italy into Graubünden, and the **golden jackal** is spreading from the east.

The return of the large predators also leads to conflicts, especially when wolves kill sheep and goats. That is why **livestock protection** with fences and guard dogs is promoted. KORA’s data help the authorities to decide on the basis of facts, for example whether an animal may be shot. The decisions themselves, however, are taken by the Confederation and the cantons.

Anyone who sees or photographs a lynx, wolf or wildcat can report it. Such **reports** from the public feed into the monitoring. On its website KORA publishes reports and maps of the distribution of the animals. In this way everyone can find out where the predators live in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: Regular surveillance, for example of how many animals of a species there are.
A camera that automatically takes a picture when an animal moves.
An animal that mainly hunts and eats other animals.
Measures that protect farm animals from predators.

gewusst: Every lynx has such a unique coat pattern that you can recognise it by it, like a fingerprint.
From a single dropping, a laboratory can often find out which wolf left it.
The lynx was exterminated in Switzerland, but today several hundred animals live again in the Jura and the Alps.

teile.einleitung: The koala is a marsupial from Australia that spends almost its whole life in eucalyptus trees. With its round, fluffy ears and large nose it looks like a teddy bear, but it is not a bear. It eats almost only eucalyptus leaves and sleeps for most of the day.
wichtigste: The koala is a marsupial and lives in the wild only in Australia.
It is considered one of the best-known symbolic animals of Australia.
It eats eucalyptus leaves and also gets most of its water from them.
A newborn baby koala is only as big as a bean.
Koalas mostly live alone and like best to move by climbing in trees.
On the ground a koala can run fast over short distances and even swim if need be.
When forests are cleared, its habitat shrinks and it finds less food.
In Switzerland you can see koalas only in a zoo.

abschnitte.text: A koala grows to about 60 to 85 centimetres and, depending on the region, weighs about 4 to 15 kilograms. Its thick fur is grey, and the ears are round and fluffy. It has strong **claws**, and on the front paws two fingers that oppose the others. In this way it can grip branches firmly.

Koalas live in the east and south-east of **Australia** in forests with eucalyptus trees. Most of the time they sit in forks of branches high up in the trees. They come down to the ground mainly to move to another tree. There they can run surprisingly fast over short distances and, if necessary, swim.

Koalas eat almost only leaves of the **eucalyptus**, and of the many eucalyptus species they like only some. The leaves are tough, low in nutrients and poisonous to many other animals. A very long caecum full of bacteria helps the koala to digest them. Because the leaves contain a lot of water, it only rarely has to drink.

Eucalyptus leaves provide only little energy. That is why a koala sleeps or rests for up to 20 hours a day. Koalas mostly live alone and have a territory of their own. In the mating season you can hear the males bellowing and grunting loudly at night.

A newborn koala is only about 2 centimetres long, as small as a bean, and still naked and blind. It crawls straight into its mother’s **pouch** and drinks milk there. After about six months it looks out for the first time. After that it rides on its mother’s back for a few more months.

Koalas lose their habitat through the **clearing** of forests for fields, roads and settlements. In the great bushfires of 2019 and 2020 many animals died. Diseases, cars and dogs also threaten them. Since 2022 the koala has officially been classed as endangered in several parts of Australia, and in Switzerland you can watch it, for example, at Zurich Zoo.

begriffe.erklaerung: A mammal whose young are born very small and grow up in the mother’s pouch.
A tree from Australia with strongly scented, oily leaves.
The part of the gut in which, in the koala, bacteria break down the hard leaves.
Felling trees and removing roots to make room for fields or houses.

gewusst: Koalas have fingerprints that look very similar to those of humans.
The koala’s pouch opens downwards towards the hind legs and not upwards as in the kangaroo.

teile.einleitung: In evolution, convergence is the independent development of similar features in species that are not related to each other. Dolphins and the extinct ichthyosaurs, for example, both have a streamlined body, although millions of years and a quite different ancestry lie between them. The reason is that the environment makes similar demands.
wichtigste: Convergence means the independent development of similar features in unrelated species.
Dolphins, sharks and ichthyosaurs all have a streamlined shape.
Dolphins are mammals, sharks are fish and ichthyosaurs were marine reptiles.
The cause is similar habitats and ways of life.
There is also convergence in plants, for example in cacti and spurge plants.
In Australia there were marsupials that closely resembled mammals of other continents.
The opposite, when related species become different, is called divergence.

abschnitte.text: The **ichthyosaurs** lived in the sea in the Mesozoic, about 250 to 90 million years ago. They had a dorsal fin, a vertical tail fin and a spindle-shaped body. Dolphins arose much later from land mammals that returned to the water. Even so, both look almost the same, because this **streamlined shape** slows them least in water.

Convergence comes from the Latin word for ‘coming together’. What is meant is that living things with different ancestors come closer to each other in their shape. Similar **environmental conditions** such as water, air or dryness lead to similar solutions. The features are then similar, but not inherited from the same ancestor.

Australia was separated from other continents for a long time, and there mainly **marsupials** developed. The extinct thylacine looked similar to a wolf or dog, although it was not related to it. The marsupial mole digs like a mole and likewise has small eyes and powerful digging hands. Sugar gliders also glide with a gliding membrane like flying squirrels.

**Cacti** grow in America, many stem-succulent spurge plants in Africa. Both have thick, green stems that store water, and spines instead of large leaves. In this way they lose little water in the heat and are not so easily eaten. In the flower shop they are hardly distinguishable, but their flowers reveal their different ancestry.

In the past, researchers classified animals mainly by their appearance. Convergence can deceive here, because a similar appearance does not always mean a close relationship. Today the **genetic material** is also compared in order to recognise true relationships. A whale, for example, is more closely related to the hippopotamus than to a shark.

About 240 million years ago there was a sea in the area of present-day Switzerland. In the region of **Monte San Giorgio** in Ticino, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, numerous fossils of marine reptiles and fish have been found. Among them are early ichthyosaurs. They show how reptiles adapted to life in the sea.

begriffe.erklaerung: The independent development of similar features in unrelated species.
An extinct marine reptile that looked like a dolphin.
A body shape that has little resistance in water or air.
When related species develop apart and become different.

gewusst: The name ichthyosaur means ‘fish lizard’, although the animals were neither fish nor lizards in the narrower sense.
Like dolphins, ichthyosaurs gave birth to live young instead of laying eggs on land.
Crab-like body shapes have arisen independently so often in crustaceans that people jokingly speak of ‘carcinisation’.

teile.einleitung: Convergent evolution means that unrelated living things independently develop similar solutions to the same problems. A famous example is the wings of birds and bats. Both can fly, but their wings came about in quite different ways.
wichtigste: Convergent evolution means that similar features develop in species of different origin.
The reason is similar living conditions and tasks, such as flying, swimming or digging.
Bird wings and bat wings are a classic example.
Such similar but independently arisen organs are called analogous.
Organs with a common origin, but often a different task, are called homologous by contrast.
Convergence shows that nature often arrives at similar good solutions.
People also use these solutions, for example in aircraft construction.

abschnitte.text: Convergent evolution, also called **convergence**, is a process in evolution. In it, species that are not closely related develop similar features. This happens because they live in similar habitats and face similar tasks. **Natural selection** then rewards in both the features that work best.

Birds, bats, the extinct pterosaurs and insects can or could all fly. In birds, feathers that sit on the arm and hand carry the wing. In bats, a **wing membrane** stretches between the very long fingers. Insect wings consist of chitin and have nothing to do with vertebrate bones at all.

Organs that have the same task but arose independently are called **analogous**. The wings of a bird and a bee are analogous. Organs with a common body plan are called **homologous**, for example the arm of a human, the leg of a cat and the wing of a bat. These have the same bones because they come from a common ancestor.

Cacti in America and some spurge plants in Africa look confusingly alike with their thick, spiny stems. Both store water because they grow in dry regions. Bats and dolphins find their way about by **echolocation**, that is, with sound that is thrown back. The camera eye, too, developed independently in vertebrates and squid.

Charles Darwin already described in the 19th century that similar ways of life can lead to similar forms. Today, by examining the **genetic material**, researchers can show exactly which species are really related. In this way it turned out that some similar-looking animals are only distantly related. Convergence is therefore important for interpreting family trees correctly.

Convergence shows that for many tasks in nature there are only a few really good solutions. Engineers are inspired by this in **biomimetics**, for example in aircraft wings or streamlined boats. For biology it is important that similarity alone does not yet prove relationship. You have to look more closely to understand where a feature comes from.

begriffe.erklaerung: The slow change of living things over many generations.
Organs with the same task but a different origin.
Organs with a common origin that often have different tasks.
Technology that takes over ideas from nature.

gewusst: Flight has developed independently at least four times in the history of the Earth: in insects, pterosaurs, birds and bats.
The eye of an octopus is very similar to the human eye, although octopuses are more closely related to snails than to us.
Hummingbirds and the hummingbird hawk-moth, a moth, also both hover in front of flowers.

teile.einleitung: The koi is a colourful ornamental fish that was bred from the carp. It is often confused with the goldfish, but it is a different relative, usually much larger. Both belong to the large cyprinid family.
wichtigste: The koi is a different, usually larger relative of the goldfish.
Koi descend from the carp, goldfish from the Prussian carp.
Koi have two pairs of barbels on the mouth; goldfish have none.
A fully grown koi often reaches 60 to 90 centimetres long.
Koi and goldfish both belong to the cyprinid family.
Koi are omnivores and often look for their food on the bottom.
Koi can live for many decades.

abschnitte.text: Koi and goldfish are both colourful ornamental fish from East Asia. The koi descends from the **carp** and was bred in Japan. The goldfish, by contrast, descends from the Prussian carp and was bred in China over a thousand years ago. Both belong to the **cyprinid** family, but are different species.

The easiest way to recognise the koi is by the **barbels**, which are two pairs of fleshy threads on the upper lip. Goldfish have no barbels. Koi usually grow much larger, often 60 to 90 centimetres, while goldfish in a pond usually reach 20 to 30 centimetres. The body of the koi is also more elongated and powerful.

Like all fish, the koi breathes with **gills**. With its barbels it feels and tastes for food in the mud. It has no teeth in the mouth, but **pharyngeal teeth** in the throat with which it crushes its food. Through the lateral line it senses movements in the water.

Koi are **omnivores**. In the wild they would eat worms, insect larvae, snails and parts of plants. In a garden pond they usually get special koi food, but also lettuce or fruit. In cold water their metabolism slows down, and they hardly eat at all.

Koi grow quickly in the first years and can later weigh several kilograms. Well-cared-for koi often live to 30 to 50 years old, some even older. In this way they often outlive their first owners. For a long life they need a large, deep and clean **pond**.

In Switzerland many people keep koi in garden ponds, and there are koi clubs and shows too. The fish survive the winter if the pond is deep enough and does not freeze over completely. Koi and goldfish must never be **released** into streams or lakes, however. There they can drive out native animals and pass on diseases.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fleshy threads at the mouth of some fish with which they feel and taste.
Teeth in the throat of cyprinids with which they crush food.
A large fish family that includes carp, koi, goldfish and roach.
A wild fish from Asia from which the goldfish descends.

gewusst: Koi and goldfish can sometimes mate with each other, but the offspring are usually infertile.
Koi often recognise the person who feeds them and swim to meet them at the edge of the pond.

teile.einleitung: Cow’s milk is the white liquid that cows produce for their calves and that we humans drink. It is one of the most important foods in Switzerland. From it come cheese, butter, yoghurt, cream and even milk chocolate.
wichtigste: A cow only gives milk after she has had a calf.
Milk consists for the most part of water.
It contains protein, fat, milk sugar, calcium and vitamins.
Milk is white because tiny particles of fat and protein scatter the light.
In Switzerland, cow’s milk is made mainly into cheese.
Heating during pasteurisation makes milk keep longer.
Some people do not tolerate the milk sugar well.

abschnitte.text: Like all mammals, a cow produces milk to feed her young. That is why she only gives milk after she has had a **calf**. The milk is made in the udder, which has four teats. A dairy cow today often gives about 20 to 30 litres of milk a day and is usually milked twice a day, often with a milking machine or a milking robot.

Cow’s milk consists of roughly 87 per cent water. The rest is **protein**, fat, **milk sugar** and minerals such as calcium, which is important for bones and teeth. Milk looks white because tiny particles of fat and protein scatter the light in all directions. If you leave raw milk to stand, the fat rises to the top and forms cream.

Fresh raw milk spoils quickly, because bacteria multiply in it. In **pasteurisation** the milk is heated briefly so that harmful germs die. The process is named after the French researcher Louis Pasteur. UHT milk, heated even more strongly, keeps unopened for several months.

In Switzerland a large part of the milk is processed into **cheese**, for example Emmental, Gruyère or Appenzeller. Butter, cream, yoghurt and quark are also made from milk. In 1875 Daniel Peter in Vevey invented milk chocolate by mixing cocoa with milk. Condensed milk and milk powder are also Swiss export products with a long history.

In Switzerland there are about half a million dairy cows, many of which spend the summer on the alp. Dairy farming is one of the most important branches of Swiss agriculture. Some people tolerate the milk sugar badly, which is called **lactose intolerance**. For them there is lactose-free milk or drinks made from plants such as oats or soya.

begriffe.erklaerung: The organ of the cow in which the milk is made.
Brief heating that kills germs and makes milk keep longer.
The milk sugar that occurs naturally in milk.
The fat-rich part of milk, called Sahne in Germany.

gewusst: For one kilogram of hard cheese such as Emmental you need about twelve litres of milk.
A cow has to eat and drink a great deal for her milk, on hot days over 100 litres of water.

teile.einleitung: Koi are colourful ornamental fish that people bred from the carp. Their home is Japan, where they have been bred in many colours and patterns for about 200 years. Today koi swim in garden ponds all over the world, including in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Koi are a colourful bred form of the carp.
The colourful koi were originally bred in Japan.
Typical colours are orange, red, white and black.
The Japanese name Nishikigoi means roughly ‘brocade carp’.
Koi can live to a great age, often several decades.
They usually grow to 60 to 90 centimetres long.
Especially beautiful koi are sold for a great deal of money.

abschnitte.text: A koi is a **bred form** of the carp. That means that over many generations people have always bred the most beautiful and colourful fish with each other. The word ‘koi’ is Japanese and simply means carp. The full name **Nishikigoi** means about the same as brocade carp, after a colourfully patterned fabric.

Breeding began in the 19th century in the **Niigata** region of Japan. Farmers there kept carp as food fish in rice-field ponds. They noticed individual fish with red and white patches, which they deliberately bred on. Koi became known all over the world after they were shown at an exhibition in Tokyo in 1914.

Koi come in many colours, above all orange, red, white, black, yellow and even metallic and shiny. Every colour combination has a Japanese name of its own. A **Kohaku** is white with red patches, a Sanke white with red and black patches. In competitions, experts judge body shape, colour and pattern.

Koi need a large, deep **pond** with clean water and a good filter system. They eat parts of plants, insect larvae, worms and special feed. In winter they become sluggish and hardly eat at all. Koi often become tame and can even be fed by hand.

Ordinary koi do not cost much, but especially beautiful animals cost a great deal. In 2018 a Kohaku was sold in Japan for the equivalent of more than a million francs. In Japan koi are a symbol of **good luck**, perseverance and strength. On Children’s Day many families hang up colourful carp streamers.

abschnitte.titel: Do not release into the wild
abschnitte.text: Koi must not be released into streams or lakes. There they can drive out native fish, tear up plants and make the water cloudy. They can also pass on diseases such as **koi herpesvirus**. Anyone who can no longer keep their koi should hand them over to a rescue centre or to other pond owners.

begriffe.erklaerung: A form of animal that has come about through deliberate selection by people.
The Japanese name of koi, in English roughly brocade carp.
A well-known koi variety, white with red patches.
A large freshwater fish from which koi were bred.

gewusst: Koi can live to 50 years and older if they are looked after well.
Every koi has a unique pattern by which you can recognise it, like a person by their fingerprint.

teile.einleitung: The Komodo dragon is the largest lizard alive today. It grows to about 3 metres long and lives only on a few islands in Indonesia. With its dangerous bite it even brings down deer and wild boar.
wichtigste: The Komodo dragon belongs to the monitor lizard family (Varanidae).
In the wild it lives only in Indonesia, on islands of the Lesser Sunda Islands such as Komodo, Rinca and Flores.
The largest animals grow to about 3 metres long, and large wild males weigh around 80 to 90 kilograms without stomach contents.
It hunts large prey and also eats carrion.
Since 2021 it has been listed as endangered on the IUCN Red List.
According to the IUCN there were fewer than 1,400 adult animals in the wild in 2021.
The Komodo National Park was founded in 1980 to protect it.

abschnitte.text: The Komodo dragon has a powerful body, strong legs with sharp claws and a muscular tail. Its skin is greyish brown and reinforced with small bony plates. With its long, forked **tongue** it picks up scents and can smell carrion from several kilometres away. It holds the record as the largest living **lizard**, with males growing clearly larger than females.

Komodo dragons live on the islands of Komodo, Rinca, Flores and a few small neighbouring islands. These belong to the **Lesser Sunda Islands** in the south of Indonesia. It is hot and dry there, with grassland, open woods and coasts. Because the islands are small, the habitat is also very limited.

The Komodo dragon is an **ambush hunter** that often waits motionless for hours beside a game trail. It preys on deer, wild boar and even water buffalo. Its bite tears deep wounds, and glands in the lower jaw release a **venom** that promotes bleeding and weakens the prey. In a single meal it can swallow a large part of its own body weight.

The female usually lays around 20 eggs in a burrow in the ground or in an abandoned nest mound. The young hatch only after about 7 to 8 months. For the first years they live mainly in trees, because large monitor lizards also eat young animals. In zoos, females have even had offspring without a male, which is called **parthenogenesis**.

In 2021 the IUCN moved the Komodo dragon up from ‘vulnerable’ to ‘endangered’. It is especially threatened by the **rising sea level** as a result of climate change, which could flood parts of its flat coastal areas. Poaching of its prey and the destruction of habitat also harm it. The **Komodo National Park**, founded in 1980, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1991.

Western science only discovered the Komodo dragon at the start of the 20th century and described it in 1912. Rumours of ‘land crocodiles’ had made researchers curious beforehand. Today it is an important attraction for tourists, who watch it with rangers. Many zoos around the world take part in breeding programmes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A scaly reptile, usually with four legs, for example a wall lizard or a monitor lizard.
A predator that waits motionless until the prey is close enough.
Reproduction without a male, from unfertilised eggs.
A list by the IUCN that shows how badly a species is threatened.

gewusst: A Komodo dragon can run briefly at up to about 20 kilometres per hour.
Young Komodo dragons sometimes roll in dung so that large members of their own species find them less appetising.
Komodo dragons are also good swimmers and can cross small stretches of sea between islands.

teile.einleitung: A cat breed is a group of domestic cats that have been bred deliberately so that they are similar in appearance and nature. There are long-haired and short-haired, large and small, even almost hairless breeds. Most cats in the world, however, do not belong to any breed.
wichtigste: Worldwide there are several dozen recognised cat breeds.
Depending on the breed association, there are between 40 and 70 breeds.
Well-known breeds are the Persian, the Siamese, the Maine Coon and the British Shorthair.
Pedigree cats have a family tree that shows their ancestors.
Most domestic cats are not pedigree cats.
Some breeding aims harm the health of the animals, which is called torture breeding.
The first big cat show took place in London in 1871.

abschnitte.text: A **breed** is a group of animals of one species that share certain features through deliberate breeding. In cats these are, for example, coat colour, coat length, body shape and head shape. For every breed there is a **breed standard** that describes exactly how the cat should look. Pedigree cats receive a family tree listing their ancestors.

Worldwide there are several dozen recognised cat breeds. Depending on the **breed association**, there are between about 40 and 70. Large associations are, for example, the FIFe in Europe and the TICA and CFA in America. Each association decides for itself which breeds it recognises.

The **Persian cat** has long, thick fur and a round face. The Siamese cat from Thailand is slender, has blue eyes and dark ears, paws and tail tip. The **Maine Coon** from the USA is one of the largest domestic cats. The Sphynx has almost no fur and the British Shorthair has plush, often blue-grey fur.

Cats have lived with people for about 10,000 years, but for a long time they were hardly bred deliberately. Only in the 19th century did people in England begin to select cats by appearance. In 1871 the first big **cat show** took place at the Crystal Palace in London. Since then many new breeds have appeared.

Some breeding aims harm the animals, which is called **torture breeding**. Persian cats with very flat noses, for example, often have breathing problems and watery eyes. Scottish Fold cats with folded ears often suffer from bone and joint problems. In Switzerland, animal protection law bans breeding that causes the animals suffering.

The vast majority of cats in Switzerland are ordinary **domestic cats** without a family tree. They are often hardy, healthy and just as affectionate as pedigree cats. Many are waiting in animal shelters for a new home. Anyone who wants a pedigree cat should choose a reputable breeder.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of animals of one species with shared features that have been bred.
A document that shows the ancestors of an animal.
A society that sets rules for breeding and recognises breeds.
Breeding in which the animals suffer because of how they look.

gewusst: The Maine Coon can grow to over a metre long from nose to tail tip.
Siamese cats are born almost white; their dark markings only develop later.

teile.einleitung: The Kruger National Park is one of the largest and most famous wildlife reserves in Africa. It lies in the north-east of South Africa on the border with Mozambique. Here you can watch elephants, lions, rhinos and Cape buffalo in the wild.
wichtigste: The park lies in the north-east of South Africa.
It is about 19,000 square kilometres in size, almost half as big as Switzerland.
The area was founded as a reserve in 1898 and became a national park in 1926.
It is named after Paul Kruger, a former president of the Boer republic of Transvaal.
All of the Big Five animals live in the park.
It is an important habitat for rhinos, which are, however, heavily threatened there by poaching.
Every year very many tourists visit it on safari.

abschnitte.text: The Kruger National Park extends across the provinces of Limpopo and Mpumalanga. From north to south it is about 350 kilometres long and on average about 60 kilometres wide. With about 19,000 square kilometres it is almost half as big as Switzerland. In the east it borders Mozambique, and in the north it reaches as far as the **Limpopo** River.

In the park live the so-called **Big Five**: elephant, lion, leopard, Cape buffalo and rhinoceros. In addition there are giraffes, zebras, hippopotamuses, crocodiles, cheetahs, hyenas and African wild dogs. There are over 140 species of mammal and several hundred species of bird. Especially many antelopes such as the **impala** can be seen everywhere.

The park consists mainly of **savanna** with grass, bushes and individual trees. Typical are acacias, mopane trees and huge baobabs in the north. Several rivers cross the area, and in the dry season many animals gather at them. In summer rain falls, in winter it is dry, and then you can see the animals especially well.

In 1898 the government of the Boer republic of Transvaal under President Paul Kruger founded the Sabie Game Reserve. At that time many animals had declined sharply because of hunting. The first game warden, James Stevenson-Hamilton, campaigned for protection for decades. In 1926 the enlarged area was declared the Kruger National Park.

For a long time the Kruger National Park was the most important area for rhinos in the world. Since about 2008, **poachers** have killed very many animals there for their horn, which is sold illegally. Rangers, dogs and helicopters are now meant to protect the rhinos. Together with parks in Mozambique and Zimbabwe, the Kruger Park forms a cross-border reserve in which animals can roam freely.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large protected area in which nature and animals are especially protected.
The five animals elephant, lion, leopard, buffalo and rhinoceros, once regarded as especially dangerous to hunt.
A warm grassland with individual trees and bushes.
The illegal hunting and killing of protected animals.

gewusst: Several thousand elephants live in the Kruger National Park.
In the park there are rest camps with huts and campsites whose gates are closed at night to protect against wild animals.

teile.einleitung: Cartilaginous fish are fish whose skeleton is made not of bone but of flexible cartilage. They include the sharks, the rays and the strange chimaeras. It is a very old group of animals that has lived in the seas for over 400 million years.
wichtigste: Sharks are cartilaginous fish because their skeleton is made of cartilage.
The three groups of cartilaginous fish are sharks, rays and chimaeras.
Cartilaginous fish have no gill cover, but open gill slits.
They have no swim bladder; a large oily liver helps them to float.
Their skin is covered with tiny teeth that feel like sandpaper.
The whale shark is the largest fish in the world and a cartilaginous fish.
Worldwide there are over a thousand species of cartilaginous fish.

abschnitte.text: Cartilaginous fish have a skeleton of **cartilage**, a firm but flexible tissue. We humans have cartilage, for example, in the nose and in the ears. Cartilaginous fish include the **sharks**, the rays and the chimaeras, also called ratfish. In all, over 1,000 species are known, almost all of which live in the sea.

Instead of a gill cover, cartilaginous fish have open **gill slits**, usually five on each side. They have no swim bladder and would slowly sink without movement. A huge, oil-rich liver gives them buoyancy, however. Their skin carries tiny **dermal denticles**, which are built in a similar way to real teeth.

The teeth of sharks stand in several rows one behind the other. When a tooth falls out, a new one moves up, so that a shark uses up thousands of teeth in its life. Sharks have an excellent sense of smell. With the **ampullae of Lorenzini** on the snout, they can even sense the weak electric fields of prey animals.

Unlike most bony fish, cartilaginous fish are fertilised inside the female’s body. Some species lay eggs in firm, leathery capsules that are found on the beach as ‘**mermaid’s purses**’. Others, such as many large sharks, give birth to live young. Cartilaginous fish usually have only a few young and grow slowly.

The **whale shark** grows to over 12 metres long and is nevertheless harmless, because it eats plankton. The great white shark is a feared hunter of seals and fish. Among the rays, the manta ray with a wingspan of several metres is especially impressive. Chimaeras mostly live in the deep sea and have large eyes and a long, thin tail.

Many sharks and rays are **threatened** today. They are caught deliberately, for example for shark fin soup, or end up as bycatch in nets. Because they have only a few young, their populations recover only slowly. There are no cartilaginous fish in Swiss lakes and rivers, but you can watch them in show aquariums.

begriffe.erklaerung: A firm but flexible tissue, such as is also found in our nose.
An open slit behind the head through which the breathing water flows out.
Tiny tooth-like scales on the skin of sharks and rays.
Sense organs on the snout of sharks that sense electric fields.

gewusst: Sharks existed before there were trees on Earth.
Shark skin used to be used for sanding wood because of its rough dermal denticles.

teile.einleitung: The ring-tailed lemur, also called the catta, is a lemur from the island of Madagascar. Unmistakable is its long tail with black and white rings. Unlike many of its relatives, the ring-tailed lemur is often on the ground and likes to sunbathe.
wichtigste: Ring-tailed lemurs live in the wild only on Madagascar.
In German they are called Katta or Ringelschwanzmaki.
Their body without the tail is about as big as a house cat.
Ring-tailed lemurs live in groups of about 5 to 30 animals.
In the group the females are in charge, while the males usually change group.
The tail is used for balancing and for signals, not for holding on.
The ring-tailed lemur is endangered, mainly because of deforestation and slash-and-burn farming.

abschnitte.text: The ring-tailed lemur has grey fur, a white face with a black muzzle and bright yellow eyes. Its body without the tail is about 40 to 45 centimetres long, roughly as big as a house cat. The bushy tail is even longer and has black and white **rings**. It is used for balancing and as a signal; the lemur cannot hold on with it.

Ring-tailed lemurs live in the wild only in the south and south-west of **Madagascar**, a large island off the east coast of Africa. They inhabit dry forests, scrubland and rocky areas. Unlike many other lemurs, they spend a lot of time on the ground. In the morning they often sit upright in the sun with their arms spread wide to warm up.

Ring-tailed lemurs live in groups of about 5 to 30 animals. The group is led by the **females**, who stay in the group they were born in for their whole lives. The males usually leave the group they were born in and join another. Through mutual **grooming** they keep clean and strengthen their bonds.

Ring-tailed lemurs have **scent glands**, among other places on the arms and wrists. With them they mark branches and paths in their territory. Males rub their tails on these glands and then waft the scent towards a rival. These so-called **stink fights** are typical of ring-tailed lemurs.

Ring-tailed lemurs eat fruit, leaves, flowers and sometimes insects, and are especially fond of the fruit of the tamarind tree. After a pregnancy of about four and a half months, a single young one is usually born. In the first days of life it clings to the mother’s belly. Later it rides on her back.

The ring-tailed lemur is **endangered**. The greatest danger is the loss of its habitat through deforestation and slash-and-burn farming. In addition, ring-tailed lemurs are hunted or caught as pets. In many zoos, including in Switzerland, ring-tailed lemurs are kept and bred in breeding programmes.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wet-nosed primate that occurs only on Madagascar.
A patch of skin that gives off a smelly substance.
Burning down forest to make fields.
Cleaning one another’s fur, which also shows friendship.

gewusst: Ring-tailed lemurs sunbathe in a posture reminiscent of a yoga pose.
In disputes over food, the females of ring-tailed lemurs usually take precedence over the males.

teile.einleitung: Claws are pointed, curved horny tips on the toes of many animals. Cats, dogs, birds and even reptiles have them. With claws you can climb, dig, hunt and defend yourself.
wichtigste: Claws consist of keratin, the same substance as our fingernails.
A house cat normally has 18 claws, five on each front paw and four on each hind paw.
Cats can retract their claws and extend them when needed.
Dogs cannot retract their claws, which is why you hear them clicking on hard floors.
Birds of prey grab their prey with powerful claws called talons.
Claws keep growing all through life and wear down with use.
The fingernails of humans are also related to claws.

abschnitte.text: A claw is a hard sheath of **keratin** that encloses the last joint of a toe. It is usually curved and tapers to a point at the front. Inside lie blood vessels and nerves, the so-called **quick** of the claw. That is why it bleeds if you cut a claw too short.

A house cat has five claws on each front paw and four on each hind paw, so 18 altogether. At rest the claws lie hidden in a skin pocket, which keeps them sharp. Only when climbing or hunting are they **extended** by tendons. The cheetah is an exception, its claws always stay slightly visible and help it when running fast, like spikes on running shoes.

Birds of prey such as the golden eagle or the common buzzard have long, very sharp claws. These feet are called **talons**. With them they grab and hold mice, fish or hares. Woodpeckers use their claws to hold on to tree trunks, and hens scratch the ground with them for food.

Moles have broad digging shovels with strong claws with which they burrow tunnels through the soil. Squirrels climb head first down tree trunks thanks to their sharp claws. Bears use their claws to dig up roots or break open bees’ nests. Sloths hang from branches for hours with their long, hook-shaped claws.

Cats like to sharpen their claws on a **scratching post**, and old layers of horn come off as they do so. Dogs that walk a lot on soft ground sometimes need their claws trimmed. Rabbits and guinea pigs must also be checked regularly. It is best to have the trimming shown to you at a vet’s practice.

begriffe.erklaerung: A firm horny substance of which claws, hair, feathers and fingernails consist.
The name for the feet with the claws in birds of prey.
A piece of furniture for cats on which they can climb and care for their claws.
The outer hard layer of the claw, which keeps growing back.

gewusst: Cats do not scratch only for care, but also leave a scent mark with the scent glands on their paws.
A sloth’s claws are so strongly curved that it sometimes even stays hanging from the branch after death.

teile.einleitung: Climate change is the warming of the Earth that today is caused mainly by people. When we burn coal, oil and natural gas, greenhouse gases get into the air and hold more heat back on Earth. This changes the living conditions of many animals, including in Switzerland.
wichtigste: Climate change is the long-term change of the climate, today mainly a warming.
The main cause is the release of greenhouse gases such as carbon dioxide by people.
Since measurements began, Switzerland has warmed about twice as strongly as the world average.
The glaciers in the Alps are clearly melting.
Warm water contains less oxygen, so a warmer lake becomes a problem for whitefish.
Many animals and plants move to higher altitudes or further north.
In the Paris Agreement of 2015, almost all countries committed themselves to limiting the warming.

abschnitte.text: The **climate** describes the weather in a place over many years. It has changed again and again in Earth’s history, for example during the ice ages. For about 150 years, however, the Earth has been warming especially fast. Worldwide it is now on average a good 1 °C warmer than before industrialisation.

Gases such as **carbon dioxide** and methane act in the air like the glass of a greenhouse. They let sunlight through but hold heat back. This natural **greenhouse effect** is what makes life on Earth possible in the first place. Because people release much more of these gases through cars, heating, factories and livestock farming, however, the effect is strengthened.

In Switzerland it has become about 2 to 3 °C warmer since measurements began in 1864. The **glaciers** have lost a large part of their ice. There are more hot days, less snow at low altitudes and more frequent heavy rain. The permafrost in the mountains is also thawing, which can make rockfalls more likely.

Fish such as whitefish, trout and grayling need cool, oxygen-rich water. **Warm water**, however, can dissolve less oxygen than cold water. In the heatwave summer of 2018, many grayling died in the Rhine near Schaffhausen because the water became too warm. In lakes the water is also mixed less well, so that oxygen can be lacking in the depths.

Many species escape the warmth and move to higher altitudes. Mountain animals such as the **rock ptarmigan** or the mountain hare, however, find less and less room there. Some migratory birds return earlier in spring, and insects hatch earlier. At the same time, warmth-loving species from the south are spreading in Switzerland.

To slow climate change, humanity has to release far fewer greenhouse gases. Renewable energies such as hydropower, sun and wind help with this. Switzerland has set itself the goal of reaching **net zero** by 2050. Everyone can also contribute, for example by cycling, taking the train instead of flying and wasting less.

begriffe.erklaerung: A gas in the air that holds heat back, for example carbon dioxide.
A gas produced when coal, oil, gas and wood are burned.
Ground that stays frozen all year round.
No more greenhouse gas is released than is removed from the air again.

gewusst: In summer the Rhone Glacier is partly covered with white sheets so that its ice grotto melts more slowly.
In the Swiss mountains today, snow lies on average several weeks less than it did a few decades ago.

teile.einleitung: Restricted breeds, in German ‘Listenhunde’ or list dogs, are dogs of certain breeds that appear on a list kept by the authorities because they are considered especially powerful or potentially dangerous. In Switzerland each canton decides for itself whether there is such a list and which rules apply to it. For these dogs, owners often need a permit or must meet special conditions.
wichtigste: List dogs are dogs of certain breeds with special keeping rules.
In Switzerland the cantons regulate which breeds are on the list.
Some cantons ban certain breeds, others require a permit.
Some cantons have no breed list at all.
Often affected are, for example, Pit Bull Terriers or American Staffordshire Terriers.
All dogs in Switzerland must be marked with a microchip and registered.
Whether a dog becomes dangerous depends strongly on training and keeping.

abschnitte.text: A list dog is a dog whose breed is on an official **breed list**. Such lists name breeds considered especially powerful and able to cause serious injuries in an attack. Frequently named are, for example, the American Pit Bull Terrier, the American Staffordshire Terrier or the Rottweiler. Crossbreeds of these breeds can also fall under them.

In Switzerland there is no uniform law for list dogs, because matters of dogs are the responsibility of the **cantons**. That is why the rules differ greatly from canton to canton. Some cantons ban certain breeds entirely, others require a **permit**, a lead requirement or a muzzle. Anyone moving house with a dog must therefore find out about the rules in the new place of residence.

After a serious accident in December 2005 in Oberglatt in the canton of Zurich, in which a child was killed by dogs, there was much discussion about dangerous dogs throughout Switzerland. Afterwards several cantons introduced stricter rules and breed lists. For a time new dog owners throughout Switzerland also had to obtain a **proof of competence** in a course. This nationwide requirement was later abolished again, but some cantons still require courses.

Anyone who wants to keep a list dog needs, depending on the canton, a permit, a good reputation and sometimes a temperament test for the dog. Every dog in Switzerland must be marked with a **microchip** and registered in a database. Owners are always responsible for making sure their dog endangers nobody. If there is a biting incident, doctors and vets must report it to the authorities.

Many experts consider breed lists too simple. They say that any dog can become dangerous if it is badly trained, tormented or neglected. Decisive, they say, are above all **training**, keeping and the responsibility of the person. Supporters argue, by contrast, that very powerful dogs do more damage in an attack and therefore need stricter rules.

Always ask the owner first before you stroke a strange dog. Do not run away screaming and do not stare a dog directly in the eyes. Leave a dog alone when it is eating, sleeping or growling. These rules apply to all dogs, whether large or small, whether a list dog or not.

begriffe.erklaerung: A register of dog breeds to which special rules apply.
Official permission from an authority.
A test in which a dog’s behaviour is assessed.
A small chip under the skin with which an animal can be clearly identified.

gewusst: In Switzerland a dog breed can be banned in one canton and allowed in the neighbouring canton.
The data on dogs in Switzerland are stored in a national database called Amicus.
Small dogs also often bite, but their bites are usually less serious.

teile.einleitung: Condors are huge vultures from the Americas that can soar for hours without flapping their wings. There are two species, the Andean condor in South America and the California condor in North America. With a wingspan of over three metres, the Andean condor is one of the largest flying birds in the world.
wichtigste: The Andean condor and the California condor belong to the New World vulture family (Cathartidae).
The Andean condor is called Vultur gryphus in science, the California condor Gymnogyps californianus.
The word ‘condor’ comes from Quechua, a language of the Andes.
The Andean condor has a wingspan of at most around 3.1 to 3.3 metres.
A male Andean condor can weigh up to about 15 kilograms.
Only the wandering albatross has an even greater wingspan.
Condors feed mainly on carrion.

abschnitte.text: The Andean condor is black with large white patches on the wings and a white **neck ruff**. Head and neck are bare, so little dirt sticks in the feathers when feeding on carcasses. Unusual for birds of prey and vultures is that the **male** is larger than the female. Adult males can be recognised at once by the fleshy comb on the head.

The Andean condor lives in the Andes from Venezuela and Colombia down to Tierra del Fuego. It nests on rock faces and also flies over coasts and grassland. The California condor today lives in California, Arizona, Utah and the north of Mexico. Both species need open landscapes with strong **updrafts**.

Condors eat almost only **carrion**, that is, dead animals such as llamas, cattle or seals and whales washed up on the coast. This makes them important health police of nature. To find food, they soar for hours on warm updrafts and mountain slopes without moving their wings. In doing so they can cover very long distances in a day.

Condors reproduce very slowly. A pair usually lays only a single egg every two years, which both parents incubate for about two months. The young bird stays dependent on its parents for a long time. In return, condors live to a great age, in zoos sometimes over 50 years.

The word condor comes from the Quechua word ‘kuntur’. The Swedish naturalist **Carl von Linné** described the Andean condor scientifically in 1758. The species name gryphus means ‘hook-nosed’, and the genus name Gymnogyps of the California condor means ‘bare vulture’. The Andean condor is a national symbol of several Andean countries and appears, for example, in the coats of arms of Bolivia, Chile, Ecuador and Colombia.

The **California condor** almost became extinct, and in 1987 only 27 animals were left. All of them were caught and bred in zoos, and since 1992 birds have been released again. A great danger to this day is **lead poisoning** from ammunition remains in carrion. The Andean condor, too, is threatened by poisoning and persecution.

begriffe.erklaerung: A vulture family from the Americas that is not closely related to the vultures of Europe.
The flesh of dead animals.
Rising air with which birds gain height without flapping.
The distance from one wing tip to the other.

gewusst: An Andean condor can soar for over five hours with almost no wingbeat at all.
The largest bird of the Swiss Alps, the bearded vulture, reaches a wingspan of almost 3 metres, nearly that of a condor.
The vultures of the Americas look similar to the vultures of Europe, but developed independently.

teile.einleitung: Cloven-hoofed animals (Klauentiere in German) are animals whose hooves are split into two parts. They include many well-known farm animals such as cows, sheep, goats and pigs. In technical language they are called even-toed ungulates.
wichtigste: Cloven-hoofed animals walk on two toes, each sitting in a hoof.
The split hooves of the cow are called cloven hooves.
A cow has two toes on each foot that touch the ground.
Cloven-hoofed animals include cattle, sheep, goats, pigs, deer and chamois.
Horses and donkeys are not cloven-hoofed; they have an undivided hoof.
Many cloven-hoofed animals are ruminants and eat grass and leaves.
In Switzerland, cloven-hoofed animals are very important for agriculture.

abschnitte.text: The German word **Klauentiere** is used mainly in farming and veterinary medicine. It means animals with split hooves. Scientifically they belong to the **even-toed ungulates**. This group includes several hundred species worldwide, from small mouse deer to the giraffe.

A cow has two large toes on each foot, the third and the fourth. Each sits in a hard horn capsule, the hoof. Behind them sit two small **dewclaws**, which help only on soft ground. The weight rests evenly on the two main toes, which gives good grip on soft ground and on slopes.

On Swiss farms the animals are mainly **cattle**, sheep, goats and pigs. In the wild they include red deer, roe deer, chamois, ibex and wild boar. Camels, giraffes and hippos are also even-toed ungulates. Horses, donkeys and zebras, on the other hand, have only one toe per foot and belong to the **odd-toed ungulates**.

Many cloven-hoofed animals such as cows, sheep, goats and deer are **ruminants**. They have a stomach with several chambers. The food is first swallowed roughly, later brought back up into the mouth and chewed thoroughly. In this way they can obtain a lot of energy from grass, which is difficult for other animals.

In Switzerland about one and a half million cattle are kept. They provide milk for cheeses such as Emmental and Gruyère as well as meat. Sheep and goats often graze on steep alpine pastures where no machines can go. For the health of cloven-hoofed animals, regular **hoof care** and dry barns are important.

If the hooves grow too long or become inflamed, the animals limp. That is why hoof trimmers trim them regularly. Feared is **foot-and-mouth disease**, a very contagious disease that affects only cloven-hoofed animals. Switzerland therefore monitors its animal stocks closely so that such epidemics do not spread.

begriffe.erklaerung: A horn shoe on a toe of an even-toed ungulate.
The scientific name for animals with two weight-bearing toes per foot.
Animals such as the horse or rhinoceros in which the middle toe bears the weight.
A plant-eater that chews its food several times and has a stomach with several chambers.

gewusst: According to current knowledge, whales descend from even-toed ungulates, and their closest living relative is the hippo.
Camels are even-toed ungulates, but walk on soft pads instead of hard hooves.

teile.einleitung: The coyote is a wild dog from North America, somewhat smaller than a wolf. It is a close relative of the wolf and the jackal and famous for its howling at night. Hardly any other animal has adapted so successfully to people; you can even find it in the middle of big cities.
wichtigste: The coyote is a close relative of the jackal and lives in North America.
It belongs to the genus of wolf-like and jackal-like canids, like the wolf and the golden jackal.
Coyotes are smaller than wolves and usually weigh 8 to 20 kilograms.
They eat almost anything, from mice and rabbits to fruit and rubbish.
Their scientific name Canis latrans means ‘barking dog’.
In the last hundred years, coyotes have spread across almost all of North America.
They also live in cities such as Chicago or Los Angeles.

abschnitte.text: The coyote is a slender wild dog with a pointed muzzle, large ears and a bushy tail. Its fur is greyish-brown to yellowish, the throat and belly lighter. It usually weighs 8 to 20 kilograms and is thus much smaller than a **wolf**. When running, it carries its tail low, the wolf more horizontally.

Coyotes live in **North America** and Central America, from Alaska and Canada to Panama. Originally they were animals of the prairies and deserts of the west. Because people wiped out many wolves and cleared forests, they spread far to the east. Today they also live in suburbs and big cities, where they usually show themselves at night.

Coyotes are very adaptable **omnivores**. They hunt mainly mice, rabbits and ground squirrels, sometimes also young deer. They also eat insects, berries, fruit and carrion. In cities they search through rubbish and sometimes catch house cats.

Coyotes live alone, as a pair or in small **family groups**. They communicate by howling, yapping and barking, which can be heard far away at night. Pairs often stay together for many years. In spring the female usually gives birth in a den to four to seven pups, and both parents look after them.

The coyote belongs to the genus **Canis**, which also includes the wolf, the golden jackal and our domestic dog. Coyotes can mate with wolves and dogs. In the east of North America there are therefore animals with wolf genes that are sometimes called ‘coywolves’. There are no coyotes in Switzerland, but for some years its relative, the **golden jackal**, has been migrating in.

In many stories of the native peoples of North America, the coyote is a clever, cunning **trickster**. Sometimes he helps people, and at other times he plays tricks on them. The name coyote comes from the Aztec language Nahuatl. It is also known as a cartoon character who tries in vain to catch a fast running bird.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wild predator from the dog family, such as the wolf, fox or jackal.
An animal that eats both meat and plants.
The genus that includes the wolf, coyote, jackal and domestic dog.
A cunning character in stories who outwits others with cleverness.

gewusst: A coyote can reach over 60 kilometres per hour when running.
When many coyotes are hunted, the females often have more young, which is why coyotes can hardly be wiped out.

teile.einleitung: Lemurs are primates, that is, relatives of monkeys and humans, that occur only on the island of Madagascar. They include over 100 species, from the tiny mouse lemur to the large indri. The best-known lemur is the ring-tailed lemur with its black and white ringed tail.
wichtigste: Lemurs live only on Madagascar and a few nearby islands.
There are over 100 species of lemur.
The best-known lemur is the ring-tailed lemur with its ringed tail.
Lemurs have a toothcomb in the lower jaw for grooming.
On the second toe of the hind feet they have a grooming claw.
In many lemurs the females are in charge in the group.
Almost all species of lemur are threatened with extinction.

abschnitte.text: Lemurs belong to the **primates**, but are not true monkeys, being so-called wet-nosed primates. They often have a long snout, large eyes and a good sense of smell. The smallest, the **mouse lemurs**, weigh only about 30 grams. The largest living lemur, the indri, weighs several kilograms and has only a short tail.

Many millions of years ago the ancestors of lemurs probably reached **Madagascar** from Africa on drifting rafts of plants. There were no monkeys there as competition, and so many different species developed. They settle in rainforests, dry forests and even thorn-scrub landscapes. In the past giant lemurs also lived on Madagascar, which grew as big as gorillas but are extinct today.

Lemurs have a special row of teeth in the lower jaw, the **toothcomb**. The incisors and canines stand there close together and flat, pointing forwards, like the teeth of a comb. With it they groom their fur and that of their group members, but they also use it when eating. In addition they have a **grooming claw** on the second toe of the hind feet, with which they scratch themselves.

The ring-tailed lemur lives in groups of about 10 to 25 animals in which the females decide. In the morning it likes to sit in the sun with arms spread to warm up. In quarrels males rub their tail with scents and wave it at the rival, which is called a **stink fight**. Unlike many other lemurs, the ring-tailed lemur is often on the ground.

The name lemur comes from the Latin word **lemures**, which is what the ancient Romans called the spirits of the dead. The Swedish naturalist Carl von Linné gave them this name, probably because of their large, shining eyes and because many are active at night. Especially mysterious is the **aye-aye** with its long, thin middle finger. With it, it taps tree bark and fishes insect larvae out of the wood.

Lemurs are regarded as the most threatened group of mammals in the world. Their forest is cleared for fields, charcoal and timber, and some are hunted. Protected areas and projects with the local people are meant to help. Zurich Zoo, too, supports a national park on Madagascar with its **Masoala Hall**, and there you can watch lemurs up close.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of mammals that includes lemurs, monkeys and humans.
Lower front teeth arranged like a comb, for grooming.
A special claw on the second toe for scratching and cleaning.
Occurring only in one particular area of the world.

gewusst: Some mouse lemurs hibernate in a way in the dry season and live on fat stored in the tail.
The indri sings loud songs that can be heard for kilometres.
The females of ring-tailed lemurs outrank the males and may eat first.

teile.einleitung: The king cobra is the longest venomous snake in the world and lives in the forests of South and South-East Asia. It eats mainly other snakes, which is why its genus is called Ophiophagus, ‘snake eater’. Since 2024, researchers have even distinguished four different species of king cobra.
wichtigste: The king cobra belongs to the elapid family (Elapidae).
It can grow to over 5 metres long and is thus the longest venomous snake.
Its main food is other snakes.
The female is the only known snake that builds a proper nest of leaves.
Theodore Edward Cantor first described it scientifically in 1836.
A revision in 2024 divided the king cobra into four species.
When threatened, it raises the front of its body high and spreads a hood.

abschnitte.text: King cobras usually grow to 3 to 4 metres long, with individual animals over 5 metres. Depending on the area, their colour ranges from olive green through brown to almost black, often with pale crossbands. When in danger, it lifts about a third of its body off the ground and spreads a **hood**, which is narrower than in true cobras. It also gives a deep hiss that sounds almost like a **growl**.

King cobras live in India, southern China, South-East Asia, Indonesia and the Philippines. They prefer dense forests, bamboo thickets and areas near water. Since 2024, four species have been distinguished, including the **Western Ghats king cobra** (Ophiophagus kaalinga) in the south-west of India and the Luzon king cobra (Ophiophagus salvatana), which occurs only on the island of Luzon. The division was published in the journal European Journal of Taxonomy.

The king cobra eats mainly other snakes, such as rat snakes, pythons and even other venomous snakes. Sometimes it also preys on monitor lizards and other lizards. Its **venom** acts mainly on the nerves and paralyses the prey. After a large meal it can manage for weeks without food.

The female pushes leaves together into a mound with her body and lays about 20 to 40 eggs in it. The warmth of the rotting leaves helps with **incubation**. The female guards the nest and defends it fiercely. The young snakes are venomous from the moment they hatch and are independent at once.

Cantor first called the genus Hamadryas, but this name had already been given to a **butterfly genus**. For that reason the zoologist Albert Günther set up the genus Ophiophagus in 1864. Hermann Schlegel had described today’s Sunda king cobra in 1837 as Naja bungarus. The species name kaalinga means ‘dark’ or ‘black’ in the Kannada language, while salvatana comes from the local name of the snake on Luzon.

King cobras are rather shy and mostly avoid people. A bite is very dangerous, however, because it can release large amounts of venom, and must be treated at once with an **antivenom**. In India and other countries the cobra plays an important part in religion and culture. Because of the felling of forests and the trade in animals, it is considered threatened.

begriffe.erklaerung: A snake family with fixed fangs at the front of the upper jaw, for example cobras and mambas.
Spread skin at the neck with which a cobra looks bigger.
A medicine that cancels the effect of a venom.
A new scientific review in which species are classified afresh.

gewusst: Although it is called a king cobra, it does not belong to the genus of true cobras (Naja).
A king cobra can rear up so high that it looks a grown person in the eyes.
Of the four species, the Luzon king cobra lives on a single island only.

teile.einleitung: Waders are birds that look for food on shores, in mud and in shallow water. They are also called wading birds because they wade through the water on their long legs. They include, for example, sandpipers, stints, plovers and the lapwing.
wichtigste: Waders are also called wading birds.
They include the green sandpiper, the wood sandpiper, plovers and the lapwing.
Many have long legs and a long, thin beak.
With the beak they probe in the mud for worms and small animals.
Many species travel thousands of kilometres every year.
In the Wadden Sea millions of waders rest on migration.
In Switzerland you see them mainly during bird migration on lake shores.

abschnitte.text: The German word Limikolen comes from Latin and means roughly ‘mud dwellers’. What is meant is a group of birds that belong to the **Charadriiformes**. These include snipe, sandpipers, stints, plovers, oystercatchers and avocets. Worldwide there are over 200 species.

Many waders have long legs with which they **wade** through shallow water. Their beaks are shaped quite differently: short as in the plover, long and curved as in the curlew or swept upwards as in the **avocet**. In this way different species look for food at different depths and get in each other’s way little. In the tip of the beak many species have touch receptors with which they feel prey in the mud.

Waders eat worms, mussels, snails, small crustaceans and insect larvae. They peck at the surface or **probe** deep in the mud. At low tide they look for food on the mudflats, at high tide they rest packed together in higher places. Some species even turn over stones to find prey underneath.

Many waders breed in the far north, for example in the tundra, and spend the winter in Africa, South America or Australia. The **bar-tailed godwit** holds a record: it flies without a break from Alaska to New Zealand, more than 11,000 kilometres. On the way many species need resting places such as the **Wadden Sea** on the North Sea. There they eat their way to fat reserves for the onward journey.

In Switzerland only a few species of wader breed, such as the lapwing and the common sandpiper. The **lapwing** used to be common, but has declined strongly because damp meadows were drained. Today conservationists protect its nests in the fields. On migration in spring and autumn, green and wood sandpipers like to rest on lake shores, for example on Lake Neuchâtel or at the Bolle di Magadino in Ticino.

Waders usually do not build a proper nest, but lay their eggs in a shallow hollow on the ground. The eggs are well camouflaged and often speckled like pebbles. The young are **nidifugous**: they leave the nest shortly after hatching and look for food themselves. The parents warn them with calls and sometimes lure enemies away with a pretended broken wing.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird that walks through shallow water to look for food.
Coastal ground that dries out at low tide and is flooded at high tide.
A young animal that can walk and feed itself shortly after hatching.
The yearly journey of birds between breeding and wintering areas.

gewusst: Some waders shrink their digestive organs before the long flight in order to be lighter.
The German name Kiebitz imitates its call.
Avocets sweep their curved beak sideways through the water as if with a scythe.

teile.einleitung: Cephalopods are sea animals whose arms sit directly on the head, hence their German name, ‘head-footers’. They include octopuses, cuttlefish, squid and nautiluses. They are regarded as the cleverest invertebrates in the world.
wichtigste: Cephalopods form a class of molluscs, which also include snails and mussels.
They include the octopus, cuttlefish, squid and nautilus.
All cephalopods live in the sea.
They have arms with suckers and a parrot-like beak.
Many can change colour in a flash and squirt out ink.
Cephalopods have three hearts and blue blood.
The extinct ammonites were also cephalopods.

abschnitte.text: Cephalopods, **Cephalopoda** in science, are a class of molluscs. Their arms grow directly on the head around the mouth. Today there are about 800 species worldwide. A distinction is made between the eight-armed ones such as octopuses, the ten-armed ones such as cuttlefish and squid, and the **nautiluses** with many small tentacles.

In the mouth sits a hard **beak** with which they crack crabs and mussels. Cephalopods have three hearts: two pump blood through the gills, one through the rest of the body. Their blood is blue because it uses copper instead of iron to carry oxygen. They have large, powerful eyes and a large brain.

Cephalopods can swim by **jet propulsion**, forcing water out of a funnel with great force. In their skin there are colour cells with which they change colour and pattern in fractions of a second. When in danger, many release a cloud of **ink** and flee. In the past the ink of the cuttlefish was even used for writing and painting.

The smallest cephalopods are only a few centimetres across. The **giant squid** can grow to over 10 metres long with its long tentacles. The colossal squid from the Southern Ocean is regarded as the heaviest invertebrate and can weigh several hundred kilograms. Both live in the deep sea and have rarely been filmed alive.

Cephalopods have existed for over 500 million years. The **ammonites** with their spiral shells died out about 66 million years ago together with the dinosaurs. Their fossils are often found, including in the Swiss Jura, which used to be a sea. Today’s nautilus still carries a shell like its ancestors.

Squid and cuttlefish are eaten in many countries, for example as fried calamari. Cephalopods are exciting for research because they learn, solve problems and remember things. Their ability to camouflage themselves inspires researchers to develop new materials. In Switzerland you can watch cephalopods, for example, in large aquariums and zoos.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal group with a soft body, for example snails, mussels and cephalopods.
Movement in which expelled water pushes the animal forwards.
An extinct cephalopod with a spiral shell.
A cup-shaped adhesive disc with which an arm can hold on.

gewusst: The eyes of the giant squid and the colossal squid can grow to over 25 centimetres and are among the largest in the whole animal kingdom.
Although cephalopods change colour so skilfully, most of them are probably colour-blind.
The word ‘sepia’ for a brown colour comes from the ink of the cuttlefish.

teile.einleitung: The salmonids are a family of fish that includes salmon, trout, char, grayling and whitefish. They mostly live in cool, oxygen-rich water. In Switzerland they are among the most important fish for fishing and cooking.
wichtigste: The salmon belongs to the salmonid family.
Whitefish also belong to the salmonids.
Typical is a small adipose fin between the dorsal fin and the tail.
Salmonids need cool, oxygen-rich water.
Many species spawn in autumn or winter on gravel beds.
In Switzerland live, among others, brown trout, lake trout, grayling, Arctic char and whitefish.
Whitefish are the most important fish for professional fishers on Swiss lakes.

abschnitte.text: The **salmonids** are a family of bony fish of the Northern Hemisphere. They include salmon, trout, char, huchen, grayling and whitefish. Their body is slim and streamlined, often with small scales and spots. A typical feature is the **adipose fin**, a small fin without spines between the dorsal fin and the tail fin.

Salmonids live in streams, rivers and lakes, some also in the sea. They need cool, clean water with plenty of oxygen. If the water becomes too warm in summer, they get into difficulty. That is why they are good **indicator species** for clean, near-natural water.

Many salmonids spawn in autumn or winter. The females beat a pit in the gravel with their tail and lay their eggs there. The males fertilise the eggs, and afterwards they are covered with gravel. The young fish hatch in spring and at first live off their yolk sac.

In Swiss streams lives the **brown trout**, in large lakes the lake trout and the Arctic char. The grayling can be recognised by its large, flag-like dorsal fin. In almost all large lakes live various kinds of **whitefish**, which, depending on the region, are also called Albeli, Balchen or Blaufelchen. They are the most important fish for professional fishing and often end up as a fillet on the plate.

Many salmonids are threatened today. Reasons are power stations, weirs, canalised streams and water that is too warm because of climate change. Disease and pollutants also affect the fish. Fish ladders, restored rivers and closed seasons are meant to help the populations.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of closely related animal species in biology.
A small, soft fin on the back in front of the tail fin.
A species of animal or plant whose presence tells you something about the environment.
Silvery salmonids that live in shoals in many Swiss lakes.

gewusst: In Swiss lakes many species of whitefish of their own have developed over thousands of years, and some occur in only a single lake.
The grayling is said to smell of thyme, which is why it is called Thymallus in science.

teile.einleitung: The cormorant is a large, dark water bird that can dive superbly and catch fish. You often see it sitting on posts or trees, spreading its wings to dry. In Switzerland it is at home on many lakes and rivers.
wichtigste: The cormorant (Phalacrocorax carbo) belongs to the cormorant family (Phalacrocoracidae).
This family is now placed in the order Suliformes, the totipalmate birds in the narrower sense.
The species name carbo means ‘coal’, because of the black plumage.
The German word Kormoran comes from the Late Latin corvus marinus, ‘sea raven’.
A cormorant is about 77 to 94 centimetres long and has a wingspan of 121 to 149 centimetres.
Adult cormorants have emerald-green eyes and a hooked beak.
Under water it drives itself along mainly with its feet.

abschnitte.text: The cormorant is black with a bluish or greenish gloss. Males typically weigh about 2 to 3.2 kilograms. The long beak has a **hooked** tip with which it holds slippery fish. In the breeding season adult birds have white patches on the head and thighs, and the **emerald-green** eyes shine all year round.

The cormorant lives on coasts, lakes and large rivers in Europe, Asia, Africa, Australia and the east of North America. It needs waters rich in fish and trees or rocks for resting and breeding. Many cormorants from the north spend the winter in central Europe. They breed in **colonies**, often with hundreds of nests in one stand of trees.

The cormorant feeds almost only on fish. It usually dives a few metres deep and stays under water for about half a minute to a minute. In doing so it paddles with its feet, on which all four toes are joined by **webbing**. In a day a cormorant eats about 400 to 500 grams of fish.

The cormorant’s plumage gets wet when diving, because it is not completely water-repellent. This gives it less buoyancy and lets it dive more easily. Afterwards it often sits with **outspread wings** on a post to dry them. This typical posture is reminiscent of a coat of arms.

The name **Phalacrocorax** is Greek, ‘phalakros’ meaning bald-headed and ‘korax’ raven. The German name comes from the Late Latin corvus marinus, that is, sea raven. In China and Japan people have fished with tamed cormorants for centuries, which wear a ring around the neck. In this way the birds cannot swallow large fish and bring them to the fisherman.

For a long time the cormorant was only a winter visitor in Switzerland. Since 2001 it has bred again, first in the **Fanel** nature reserve on Lake Neuchâtel. Today there are colonies on several lakes, above all on large lakes in the Central Plateau. Because it eats many fish, there are conflicts with professional fishers, and the cantons may regulate the population under certain conditions.

begriffe.erklaerung: The family of water birds to which the cormorant belongs.
Skin between the toes that works like a paddle when swimming.
A group of birds that breed close together.
The force that pushes a body upwards in water.

gewusst: When cormorants breed in large colonies, their droppings can make the trees beneath the nests die.
Cormorants often fly in a V formation or in long lines just above the water.
Cormorants can see well under water because the lens of their eye can change shape strongly.

teile.einleitung: Coevolution means that two species of living things change together and adapt to each other over a very long time. A well-known example is flowers and the insects that pollinate them. Every change in one species influences the development of the other, like a dance in which both partners react to each other.
wichtigste: In coevolution, two species develop over a long time in a way that is matched to each other.
A classic example is flowers and their pollinating insects.
Coevolution occurs between partners that benefit each other and between opponents such as predator and prey.
Because of an orchid, Charles Darwin predicted a moth with an extremely long proboscis.
The researchers Paul Ehrlich and Peter Raven made the term coevolution well known in 1964.
Parasites and their hosts also influence each other’s development.
Coevolution explains many astonishing adaptations in nature.

abschnitte.text: Evolution is the slow change of living things over many generations. In **coevolution**, two species adapt to each other. What is an advantage for one species depends on the behaviour or body of the other. The term was made known by the American researchers Paul Ehrlich and Peter Raven in 1964, who studied butterflies and their food plants.

Flowers offer insects **nectar** and pollen as food. In return the insects carry the pollen to the next flower and pollinate it. Over millions of years, the shape, colour and scent of flowers have adapted to their visitors. Bumblebees with a long tongue, for example, visit flowers with deep tubes that are out of reach for short-tongued insects.
